name: Arsveil (open world)
author: Story Suite examples
description: Arsveil: the world of Ersveil (the same places, routes, realms, powers, lore and world events) with its own cast. Until the new cast is written, the people are Ersveil's, as placeholders. A new story begins at the Adventurer Guild office in Bluewatch Village on 1 October CY 611.

places.name: Highmark Capital
places.note: Imperial throne city of walled districts; seals, legal services and arms contracts.

places.name: Highmark Capital / Crown Keep
places.note: Palace, Diet and War Office; imperial warrants and sealed petitions.

places.name: Highmark Capital / Noble Heights
places.note: Walled noble estates: tailors, fine tack, household retainers.

places.name: Highmark Capital / Knight Quarter
places.note: Barracks and tilting yards; arms repair, cavalry tack, officer lodging.

places.name: Highmark Capital / Civic Ward
places.note: Tax courts, guildhalls and tenements; daily provisions and common lodging.

places.name: Iron Guard Fortress
places.note: Main imperial stronghold; armour repair and siege stores.

places.name: Barak Freeport
places.note: Highmark's southern port at the head of the Barak Gulf; Belis River freight lands here.

places.name: Oathmere
places.note: Highmark lake town of horse breeders and fishers (the lake of the same name lies beside it).

places.name: Stoneford
places.note: Fortified road town on the way to Barak; wagon repair, base for the Southmarch Road.

places.name: Ravenholt
places.note: Western border fortress at the head of the Barrens caravan road; raider watch.

places.name: Thornwall Redoubt
places.note: The Wardens of the Last Wall's fortress on Highmark's northern march, where the roads from the Border Kingdoms and Valegard meet; the Last Wall's earthworks run east and west from it.

places.name: Thousand Sails
places.note: River Council seat and fleet hub; bulk cargo and contract brokers.

places.name: Thousand Sails / Council Quay
places.note: River Council chambers and toll courts; charters and contract witnesses.

places.name: Thousand Sails / Grand Bazaar
places.note: Wholesale market and warehouses; bulk imports and foreign merchant courts.

places.name: Thousand Sails / Hulkrow
places.note: Old barges moored together as floating slums for the poor and those in hiding.

places.name: Ledgerford
places.note: Banking city: assay, deposits, bank notes, sealed contracts.

places.name: Ledgerford / Vault Row
places.note: The great banks behind armed vaults.

places.name: Ledgerford / Assay Hall
places.note: Every coin weighed, every note honoured or refused.

places.name: Ledgerford / Debtors' Steps
places.note: Public auctions of debts, collateral and bondfolk.

places.name: Bluewatch Village
places.note: Northernmost village: river watchpoint, Auvoth convoy supplies, cold-weather gear.

places.name: Bluewatch Village / Guild Office
places.note: Adventurer Guild branch desk where new arrivals register and read the job board.

places.name: Mirage City
places.note: Pleasure city of theatres, auctions and gambling credit.

places.name: Coinwater
places.note: Confederacy mint city; coin assay and sealed freight receipts.

places.name: Saltledger Quay
places.note: Estuary port: salt, fish, sea-river customs and pilot contracts.

places.name: Glassdock
places.note: Port for fragile cargo where the Bluewatch Branch meets the Glassdock Channel.

places.name: Lowmarket Reach
places.note: Caravan entry to Confederacy markets; freight transfer and Mirage-road guides.

places.name: Floodbell
places.note: Floodgate town: levee tools, emergency grain; second approach to Drowned Bell Vault.

places.name: Brightwater Lock
places.note: Fortified customs lock on the northern Ledger; gateway to Chainlock Depths.

places.name: Ferrywake
places.note: Ferry-chain town; start of the causeway to Drowned Bell Vault.

places.name: Marshledger
places.note: Estuary accounting town: salt and fish accounts, pilot contracts.

places.name: Shorn
places.note: Ducal capital and Confederacy bastion on the road to Auvoth.

places.name: Old Lantern Post
places.note: Shrine-town at the edge of settled land; lamp oil, trail blessings, wayfarer shelter.

places.name: Hearthmere
places.note: Hot-spring refuge town with bathhouses, winter lodging and reserve granaries.

places.name: Greyvein Camp
places.note: Mining camp and gateway to the Rimeglass Galleries; cold iron, blue coal, dungeon permits.

places.name: Frostgate
places.note: Last lock before Shorn and head of navigation; sledges beyond.

places.name: Rimebridge
places.note: Toll fortress tying Shornmarch to Ledgerford; convoy papers, guarded warehousing.

places.name: Wolfmere Outpost
places.note: Scout post on the Auvoth bastion road; reports, remounts, escort hire.

places.name: Hollin's Reach
places.note: Northernmost Shornmarch village; wool, mutton and hay by barter, little coin.

places.name: Auvoth
places.note: Guild-governed megadungeon city and Guild capital; charts, adventurer gear, salvage, dear food and beds.

places.name: Auvoth / Seventh Seal Terrace
places.note: The tower over the seventh seal: courts and sealed descents; arbitration, permits and seal services.

places.name: Auvoth / Sealcrown
places.note: Guild Grand Hall ward: dungeon contracts, charts, adventurer lodging.

places.name: Auvoth / Outer Lamps
places.note: Southern gate ward: entry, convoy inspection, last-minute supplies.

places.name: Auvoth / Pale Market
places.note: Restricted salvage market: sealed auctions, forbidden salvage.

places.name: Auvoth / Boneglass Yard
places.note: Monster-material workshops: bone craft, iceglass, custom adventurer gear.

places.name: Auvoth / Ashbell Hospice
places.note: Hospital ward: wound care, amputation, frostbite and antidotes.

places.name: Holy City of Aurelion
places.note: Sacred capital around the First Brazier; relic craft, funerary goods, Church legal services.

places.name: Holy City of Aurelion / First Brazier
places.note: The sacred flame that never went out; authorised offerings and ritual appointments.

places.name: Holy City of Aurelion / Cathedral of the Eternal Flame
places.note: High cathedral and public doctrinal court; clerical records and petitions.

places.name: Holy City of Aurelion / Ashen Steps
places.note: Funeral stairs where the dead are carried up; urns, mourning cloth, procession services.

places.name: Holy City of Aurelion / Sepulcher of Saints
places.note: Saint tombs and sealed crypts under grave-warden watch.

places.name: Holy City of Aurelion / Great Reliquary
places.note: Fortified custody of relics; authentication and armed transfers.

places.name: Holy City of Aurelion / College of Flame Theologians
places.note: Clerical school and archive; manuscripts and doctrine instruction.

places.name: Holy City of Aurelion / Silent Cloisters
places.note: Monastic copying rooms and herb gardens; closed retreats under Inquest watch.

places.name: Holy City of Aurelion / Pilgrim Courts
places.note: Pilgrim lodging, communal meals and hearings.

places.name: Gravewarden Hold
places.note: Fortified abbey-town containing undead; grave seals and burial-patrol contracts.

places.name: Mercywell
places.note: Hospital town of monastic healers and plague quarantine; gateway to Ember Reliquary.

places.name: Saint Orven's Ford
places.note: Pilgrim ford on the Marrow; guides and ferry; gateway to the Drowned Cloister.

places.name: Davenford
places.note: Ulf River bridge town with noble customs; gateway to Briarhorn Labyrinth.

places.name: Mosskar
places.note: Gate-town at the south end of the Thornroad; mules and pass guides.

places.name: Coldwick
places.note: Frontier town of furs, trackers and warning bells; gateway to Wolfcairn Deeps.

places.name: Elderwall
places.note: Town on old imperial ruins; reclaimed stone, salvage licences, mountain road to Kraghollow.

places.name: Northcairn
places.note: Cairn-town for frontier war dead; memorial stone, winter stores.

places.name: Isbro
places.note: Ulf bridge and winter toll town; the river freezes hard.

places.name: Kvildal
places.note: Pilgrim and healing town: salves, rest-houses, snow-road guides.

places.name: Ironanvil Citadel
places.note: Principal dwarven forge-city and seat of the Council Beneath Stone; masterwork arms.

places.name: Ironanvil Citadel / Molten Core Great Forge
places.note: Never-cold central forge and dwarven mint; clan commissions and masterwork repair.

places.name: Ironanvil Citadel / Hall of Names
places.note: Ancestor stones of every clan; the Citadel's own hall.

places.name: Deepmantle Hold
places.note: Clanhold city of mithril veins; gateway to Deepmantle Hollow.

places.name: Thundershaft
places.note: Summit fortress below Thunderpeak; climbing gear and cold stores.

places.name: Windcutter Pass
places.note: High pass on the Ironanvil Mountain Road between Gateward Fortress and Gavrund; closes for weeks in deep winter, months in a hard winter.

places.name: Battle Cry City
places.note: Chieftain Council and Grand Muster city; warband contracts, plains mounts.

places.name: Battle Cry City / Muster Ground
places.note: Where the clans gather for war.

places.name: Battle Cry City / Fire Circle
places.note: Where the Chieftain Council speaks law.

places.name: Ancestral Spirit Mesa
places.note: Sacred mesa-town of clan rites and oath gatherings.

places.name: Fangmarket
places.note: Market of hides, leather and monster trophies; saltpeter is for tanning, preservation, dyeing and alchemy only (no gunpowder).

places.name: Talon Perch
places.note: Cliff town of griffin scouts; gateway to Skyclaw Eyrie.

places.name: Hurrakai
places.note: Fortified southern clan town on the Barak Gulf shore; start of the Coastway.

places.name: Abysswatch
places.note: Covenant council seat and naval command on a sea-fort rock; gateway to Leviathan Ribmaze.

places.name: Abysswatch / Fleet Basin
places.note: Warship docks and ropewalks.

places.name: Abysswatch / Admiralty Rock
places.note: Tidal Council and fleet command.

places.name: Vortex Port
places.note: Pirate refuge and smugglers' harbour.

places.name: Breakwater Hold
places.note: Fortified anti-pirate port; the Abyssal Gate route ends here.

places.name: Lanternshoal
places.note: Mainland lighthouse town: reef pilots, fog bells, emergency ship stores.

places.name: Blackvolc Isle
places.note: Volcanic isle of sulfur, obsidian and fire crystals; gateway to Blackglass Caldera.

places.name: Blackmast
places.note: Privateer port: prize cargo and illicit sea contracts.

places.name: Old Anchor Fort
places.note: Sea fortress; start of the Ghost Fleet Passage.

places.name: Atlantis
places.note: Deep-sea capital under a magical dome; coral craft and pressure-safe gear.

places.name: Atlantis / Tidevoice Plaza
places.note: Central ritual square; offerings and public proclamations.

places.name: Atlantis / Coralya's Crown
places.note: Royal district on the procession route; royal commissions.

places.name: Atlantis / Shellward Ring
places.note: Defensive ward-ring inside the dome; warded diving armour and patrol supplies.

places.name: Atlantis / Luminous Coral Ward
places.note: Craft ward of Sea-Light fragments, coral artisans and dome lamps.

places.name: Atlantis / Pearlquiet
places.note: Noble ward of elder families; fine pearls and private arbitration.

places.name: Atlantis / Abyssal Gate
places.note: Dome-gate for trench patrols; deep-sea permits, pressure gear, trench charts.

places.name: Atlantis / Singing Sand Bank
places.note: Ritual district for sacred sand and tide-chants.

places.name: Moonwhisper Ruins
places.note: Sacred ruin-city on Mirror Lake; digging permits and moonstone craft.

places.name: Starwater Quay
places.note: Mirror Lake port: moonstone, lake boats; elven end of the Rainbow Bridge.

places.name: Aurelith
places.note: Hollow-town of mana-lens artisans and message stones; gateway to Rootbound Observatory.

places.name: Greenveil Gate
places.note: Controlled gate into the elven lands; entry permits and approved guides.

places.name: Anwyth Sanctuary
places.note: Sacred grove of ancient trees and treaty stones.

places.name: Tearlight Waterfall
places.note: Sacred healing and purification waterfall.

places.name: Startrace Tower
places.note: Independent academy-city: books, instruments, research services, tutors.

places.name: Startrace Tower / Tower of Origin
places.note: Central archive, observatory and ritual hall; appointments only, no retail.

places.name: Startrace Tower / Ring of Foundation
places.note: Inner ring of dormitories, smithies, markets and storage courts.

places.name: Startrace Tower / Ring of Knowledge
places.note: Academy ring: lecture halls, libraries, laboratories.

places.name: Startrace Tower / Ring of Trials
places.note: Training ring of warded chambers, mock ruins and duelling grounds.

places.name: Startrace Tower / Oasis Gate
places.note: Caravan gate: water inspection, desert guides, entry permits.

places.name: Startrace Tower / Scholar's Rest
places.note: Inns, scribes, tutors and translators.

places.name: Startrace Tower / Glasswell
places.note: Mana-glass lenses, gauges and precision instruments.

places.name: Startrace Tower / Parchment Row
places.note: Copyists, binders and sealed scrolls.

places.name: Shackles City
places.note: Criminal-mercantile free city, a warren about 10 km across: smuggled cargo, false papers, mercenaries, debt brokers.

places.name: Dustbell
places.note: Western Barrens gate settlement affiliated with Shackles City: caravan checkpoint and mercenary hiring.

places.name: Westchain Hold
places.note: Fortified militia settlement guarding the Shackles-facing Barrens approach; gateway to Chain-Eater Pit.

places.name: Shackles City / Veil Market
places.note: Hidden market under the inner wards: stolen relics, forbidden maps, discreet appraisal.

places.name: Shackles City / Rust-Corroded Pipes
places.note: Tunnels under the old aqueducts; thieves' guild ground and smuggler passage.

places.name: Shackles City / Mute Sparrow Ward
places.note: Tavern ward and front for underground dealings; rumours and cheap beds.

places.name: Shackles City / Chainmarket
places.note: Slave and bond auctions beside contraband and stolen cargo.

places.name: Shackles City / Red Lock Quay
places.note: Riverward night smuggling quay; forged manifests.

places.name: Shackles City / Knifeglass Alley
places.note: Pit schools and pit fights, mercenary hiring; brokers and forgers in the back lanes.

places.name: Shackles City / Broken Coin Yard
places.note: Debt district of pawn courts and bonded-labour brokers (a name, not a coin).

places.name: Bloodbound Camp-City
places.note: Central mercenary contract camp; escrow, credit, sealed contracts.

places.name: Widow's Coin
places.note: Market town of death-pay claims and armour resale; a place name, not a coin.

places.name: Veilgrave
places.note: Hidden cult town under a ruined abbey; forbidden texts and hidden passages.

places.name: Black Prayer Hollow
places.note: Cursed town of heretical rites and grave pits.

places.name: Gallowsmere
places.note: Marsh town of corpse-lights and undead smuggling.

places.name: Ashpit Cloister
places.note: Ruined cloister-town trading forbidden texts and illicit cargo.

places.name: Lazar's End
places.note: Abandoned plague town now cult-held; gateway to Mournroot Catacomb.

places.name: Quiet Yard
places.note: Grave-town with a hidden ossuary market.

places.name: Wellscar
places.note: Well town controlling rare reliable water.

places.name: Dusthaven
places.note: Caravan town for Barrens crossings; water allotments and guides.

places.name: Redglass
places.note: Mining town of red sand glass; gateway to Redglass Labyrinth.

places.name: Cairnwatch
places.note: Watch town near the battlefield routes; ghost wards, scavenger permits.

places.name: Mirage Rest
places.note: Road-town tied to Mirage Spring rumours; not the true oasis.

places.name: Mirage Spring Oasis
places.note: Demiplane oasis that cannot be sought; this point is only an approximate manifestation anchor.

places.name: Wailford
places.note: Battlefield-edge town of ghost wards and relic scavengers; gateway to the Wailing Crown Vault.

places.name: Black Cistern
places.note: Fortified water town over an underground reservoir.

places.name: Stirrup Crossing
places.note: Crossing town and escort station; gateway to Pilgrim's Descent.

places.name: Echohammer
places.note: Mining town of cave-rescue crews; gateway to Echo Sink.

places.name: Witchwood Forest Center
places.note: Neutral magical forest about 100 km across under perpetual mist; navigation needs a Moonlight Compass.

places.name: Thunderpeak Summit
places.note: Storm peak above Thundershaft; no road, only climbing routes.

places.name: Winged Beasts Firmament
places.note: Floating-island Wildzone and flyers' roost; reached by air only.

places.name: Wailing Battlefield Edge
places.note: Cursed battlefield edge; ghost soldiers walk on moonless nights.

places.name: Silent Giant Necropolis
places.note: Behemoth remains with life crystals gatherable at the outer ribs.

places.name: Sea of the Ghost Fleet
places.note: Cursed sea where the ghost armada rises on moonless nights and storms; shares a coordinate with Nameless Isle on purpose.

places.name: Nameless Isle
places.note: Fog-wrapped isle at the heart of the Ghost Fleet sea; shares the sea's coordinate on purpose.

places.name: Island of Lost Time
places.note: Restricted ruin island of time-disorientation.

places.name: Abyssal Throat
places.note: Black-rock atoll around a sealed colossal pit; special sea region near Atlantis routes.

places.name: Glass Howl Icefield
places.note: Icefield of the apex direwolf Vaulkir; gateway to Sunless Crevasse.

places.name: Sunless Crevasse
places.note: Subglacial fissures with lich-type undead; forbidden expedition dungeon. Clearance SS-SSS; creature type alone sets no level or EG.

places.name: Crownless Glacier
places.note: Glacier of dragon signs, storm auroras and vanishing patrols.

places.name: Iron-Blue Tundra
places.note: Frozen apex tundra with giant elk, snow ogres and crystal-insect colonies.

places.name: Hollow Aurora Zone
places.note: Deep Wildzone under the circling light of the Pale Orbit.

places.name: Osterhal
places.note: Ardelian capital of nine peoples' quarters; imperial charters and election-season trade.

places.name: Osterhal / Ninefold Hall
places.note: Where the electors meet and emperors are chosen.

places.name: Osterhal / Citizens' Market
places.note: Food and craft of nine peoples.

places.name: Osterhal / Captive Yards
places.note: Sale yards for war captives, outside the walls.

places.name: Nareth
places.note: Dead city where no sound carries; Ardelian patrols turn travellers back.

places.name: Sorrowfen
places.note: Great marsh east of Ardelia.

places.name: Thornheart
places.note: Deep forest between Ardelia and Verdantleaf.

places.name: Vargate
places.note: Underworld harbour city of ward lords, slave factors and information brokers.

places.name: Vargate / Drowned Steps
places.note: Half-flooded lower harbour of smugglers and fences.

places.name: Vargate / Factor's Row
places.note: Slave factors' houses and holding pens.

places.name: Vargate / Silk Wards
places.note: Pleasure wards run by ward compacts, each on its own terms.

places.name: Vargate / Tolerated Ward
places.note: The Ashen Veil's tolerated temple and its buyers.

places.name: Glassmouth
places.note: Last waystation at the Barrens edge; Glass Road caravan staging.

places.name: The Glass Pits
places.note: Ashkaran slave pits on the wastes' western edge; no open market.

places.name: Ashkar
places.note: Ashkaran capital of mirrored glass, seat of the Glass Regent.

places.name: Ashkar / Regent's Mirror
places.note: The Glass Regent's palace of fused glass.

places.name: Ashkar / Bright Market
places.note: Glass-steel, slaves and western luxuries under sun-veils.

places.name: Ashkar / Pit Road
places.note: Start of the road east to the Glass Pits; Pit Road is also the corridor name.

places.name: Auvoth Depths
places.note: The largest known leyline: a sealed descent of stacked worlds under Auvoth, each band its own land with its own light, weather, seasons, prey and predators; recorded parties only. Clearance F-SSS (band 1 F-E, band 2 D); permits 2-4 silver a day for band 1, 6-12 for band 2; the Guild takes a tenth of salvage.

places.name: Auvoth Depths / The Lanternwood
places.note: Band 1 (clearance F-E): a forest lit by glowing mana veins in a stone sky, with its own day of brightening and dimming; the most worked band, full of salvage camps.

places.name: Auvoth Depths / The Underbright Sea
places.note: Band 2 (clearance D): a lightless salt sea under a sky of drifting mana motes; islands, the wrecks of earlier parties, things that hunt by sound.

places.name: Auvoth Depths / The Deep Bands
places.note: Band 3 and below (clearance unknown): known only from broken records and survivors who will not talk about them.

places.name: Rimeglass Galleries
places.note: Seasonal licensed dungeon of moving ice galleries; Shornmarch licence 2-4 silver a day. Clearance C-B.

places.name: Briarhorn Labyrinth
places.note: Ducal-licensed thicket maze of regrowing passages and briar beasts. Clearance E-D.

places.name: Wolfcairn Deeps
places.note: Restricted border dungeon of pack predators, false trails and old war wards. Clearance C-B.

places.name: Crownscar Catacombs
places.note: Licensed imperial catacombs of animated guardians and unstable lower vaults. Clearance E-D.

places.name: Drowned Bell Vault
places.note: Chartered flooded dungeon of flash floods and undertow; water stones and old bronze. Clearance E-D.

places.name: Chainlock Depths
places.note: Lockmaster-chartered dungeon of pressure chambers and hostile constructs. Clearance D-C.

places.name: Ember Reliquary
places.note: Church-sealed reliquary vaults of sanctified traps; limited access under escort. Clearance D-C.

places.name: Saint Orven's Drowned Cloister
places.note: Church-licensed flooded ruin of collapsing crypts and drowned undead; old gold votives need assay before valuing. Clearance E-D.

places.name: Deepmantle Hollow
places.note: Clan-sealed high dungeon of living stone and sealed golems. Clearance B-A.

places.name: Echo Sink
places.note: Mapped guild dungeon of sound loops, shaft collapses and blind predators. Clearance D-C.

places.name: Pilgrim's Descent
places.note: Guarded holy-order dungeon of restless dead in narrow burial shafts. Clearance E-D.

places.name: Witchwood Rootwell
places.note: Witch-restricted living dungeon of rearranging roots and memory fog. Clearance B-A.

places.name: Fallen Meridian Vault
places.note: Academy-licensed research dungeon of spatial distortion and failed constructs. Clearance C-B.

places.name: Chain-Eater Pit
places.note: Illicit contested dungeon of unstable bindings and scavenger gangs. Clearance D-C.

places.name: Redglass Labyrinth
places.note: Caravan-chartered dungeon of mirage chambers, heat and burrowing predators. Clearance C-B.

places.name: Wailing Crown Vault
places.note: Forbidden battlefield dungeon; dense mana animates the dead ("high undead" is a taxonomy, not a level or EG). Clearance A-S.

places.name: Mournroot Catacomb
places.note: Cult-held catacomb of necromancers, intelligent undead and plague chambers. Clearance B-A.

places.name: Stormhoof Barrow
places.note: Clan-licensed ancestral barrow of territorial spirits and burrowing beasts. Clearance D-C.

places.name: Skyclaw Eyrie
places.note: Aerial-contract dungeon of wind shear and sheer drops, reached by cliff trail or griffin carry. Clearance C-B.

places.name: Leviathan Ribmaze
places.note: Tide-limited licensed sea dungeon of flooding passages and crushing tides. Clearance C-B.

places.name: Blackglass Caldera
places.note: Covenant-restricted volcanic dungeon of eruptions, toxic vents and fire monsters. Clearance B-A.

places.name: Drowned Archive
places.note: Atlantis-restricted deep dungeon of crushing depth and failing wards. Clearance A-S.

places.name: Rootbound Observatory
places.note: Enclave-sealed research dungeon of guardian roots and altered senses. Clearance C-B.

places.name: Mirrorroot Maze
places.note: Restricted ruin dungeon of reflection doubles and mana mirages, reached by boat. Clearance B-A.

places.name: Root-Tyrant's Range
places.note: Roaming range of the Root-Tyrant, centred on Thornheart; its presence is never guaranteed.

places.name: Mother of Reeds' Range
places.note: Roaming range of the Mother of Reeds, centred on Sorrowfen; marsh villagers leave offerings.

places.name: Black Trawl's Range
places.note: Roaming range of the Black Trawl at the margins of the Ghost Fleet sea.

places.name: Vaulkir's Range
places.note: Territory of the apex direwolf Vaulkir the Pale Maw on the Glass Howl Icefield.

places.name: Pale Orbit's Range
places.note: Sky above the Hollow Aurora Zone where the Pale Orbit circles; patrols that go out under it do not return.

lore.title: Premise and Tone
lore.text:
Arsveil is a brutal, unkind world that takes everything from those who would survive it. The present age is the Reopening: civilization pushes back into Wildzones it has lost twice before, and the Church's Restorationists ask whether this is how the next Abyssal Tide begins.
Tone: grimdark. Everything has a price (help, passage, healing, information, even a proper death): coin, favor, risk or time. Kindness is real too: some people help because they are decent, and then the price is what it costs them, not what they ask back. The world is cruel; not every person in it is. Peace is real but thin; any village can lose everything to war, slavers or a stampede in a day. Wonders are remote, costly, almost fantastical.
Narration is explicit and direct: violence, injury, death, cruelty, slavery and sex shown plainly, never softened; sexual content involves adults only. Death is common; named characters, companions included, can die for good.

lore.title: Causality and Pressure
lore.text:
- Hostility, tests, coincidence, awe and fear need a reason inside the world. React to a messenger's news, not the messenger's strength.
- Every scene sits inside at least one active pressure (debt, hunger, tax, faction agenda, monster movement, war rumor, slavers, weather); NPCs pursue their own needs on screen. Quiet is allowed; empty is not.
- When an NPC helps, show what it costs them; some expect something back, some do not.
- A solved problem stays solved unless something with a reason and a way to know acts on it. Consequences need causes and information channels, not a quota.
- Factions, monsters and people act off screen. Major events (wars, stampedes, coups, outbreaks) come every few months to years, from causes, never on a schedule. Great threats follow causes too: what people do, {{user}} included, can hasten, delay or turn them, at whatever those deeds cost.
- The world does not scale to {{user}}: any scene may hold someone far stronger or weaker.
- No plot armor: {{user}} and companions can lose, be maimed or die when the odds say so.

lore.title: Classification
lore.text:
Three scales that never convert into one another:
- Level (1-99): raw supernatural capacity, invisible; estimated from feats, bearing, gear, scars. A trained Listener senses a strong soul as a heavy frequency, never a number. The great apexes stand above it.
- Guild Rank (F to S; SS unheld, SSS was Veyr the Unbound's alone): the Guild's certification of record and competence, not power. It can lag, be forged or go unrecognized abroad.
- Ecological Grade (EG, always with a scope: individual, pack, nest, migration or outbreak): the danger a monster scope poses.
Every soul awakens to Level 1 by adolescence; the Hollow-born never do. Physical Affinity (body reinforcement) is common, Mana Affinity (projected magic) rarer. Most adults plateau at levels 5-25.
Typical level by role (to generate people, never a conversion): townsfolk, laborers, clerks 5; militia, watch, ordinary hunters 5-15; soldiers, mercenaries, working adventurers (E-D) 10-29; sergeants, knights, Guild veterans (C), journeyman mages 30-39; order champions, elite adventurers (B-A), masters of a tradition 40-59; kingdom champions, grandmasters, S-rank legends 60-69; level 70 and above, a handful alive, named in lore.
Strength gathers where danger is: frontiers, Auvoth and Wildzone edges hold more level 25-35 people than the safe interior.

lore.title: Currency
lore.text:
Three coins only: copper; silver, worth 10 copper; gold, worth 100 copper (10 silver). Write amounts as gold, silver and copper (2g 4s 6c). There are no other coins; Ledgerford's bank notes stand for coin and are not a fourth one.
An unskilled laborer earns 16-30 copper a day, a town guard 3-6 silver. Coin is physical and heavy; clipped or counterfeit coin is refused. Haggling moves a price by a tenth to a quarter; Church, Guild and state fees are fixed. Used gear sells at 40-70% of new; fine work costs 2-4 times, masterwork 5-10 times. Prices never scale with the buyer's power or reputation. Sapient beings are never livestock. Specialists cluster in cities, temples, academies and Guild centers; a frontier village may have no healer at any price.

lore.title: Authority and Generation
lore.text:
Sources: this lorebook, the pack (map, routes, calendar, weather, events; standing, fame, Guild records) and the extensions' records.
- Metaphysics (souls, death, mana, primordials, how magic works) never changes; everything else (laws, institutions, borders, prices, customs) is a default that confirmed campaign events can change. For changeable facts: story events > tracked records (scene block, inventory and purse, Director note, NPC dossiers) > lore and pack defaults.
- Characters know only what they saw, were told, read or could guess; the narrator knows the lorebook, NPCs do not. Levels are never seen as numbers.
- Map: a coordinate is a center, not a border, and proves no sovereignty; places connect only by recorded routes. Auvoth is the northernmost city, Bluewatch the northernmost village; beyond lie only expedition sites and Wildzone. Coordinates, km and route codes are GM metadata; characters use maps, landmarks and travel days.
- Open world: the pack lists no items, shops, prices, foes or jobs. Create them from the lore (Currency, wages, prices, the Bestiary, the Guild); once named in play they keep their identity. Gear, coin and wounds come only from what happened in the story.
- Unmapped space is not empty: freely create villages, farms, shrines, camps, ruins and minor roads, never reusing a name. Invented places never create major crossings, trunk routes or passes through barriers. Roads built, opened or destroyed in play become canon. Build every new name from the Names entries, never a stock fantasy name (Elara, Kael, Thorne, Millbrook).
- Sealed truths are never answered by anyone (which primordial the First Tide threatened, Veyr's fate, where otherworlders come from, what silenced Nareth, the bottom of the Auvoth Depths, the floor of Nyara's prison). They open only through explicit campaign events (the approach to the Hall of Heroes, the Iron Archive piece by piece, the heart of the Nameless Isle). An 'Unknown:' line in a site or apex entry is an ordinary mystery unless marked sealed or listed here: nobody outside it knows or tells, and play uncovers it only through campaign events. Ordinary secrets are held by named people and learnable by plausible means.

lore.title: Knowledge and Reputation
lore.text:
- Deeds need witnesses; what happens in the wilderness with no one alive to tell it stays unknown. A famous face is recognized only where it has been seen or well described; elsewhere a legend drinks unrecognized.
- Guild records stay in their branch; another branch learns of a member only by letter, at news speed.
- Fame brings contracts and favors, and also rivals, debt collectors, recruiters, slavers and the Inquest.
- An NPC knows a secret only if lore or their dossier names them as knowing it, or they learned it in play.
- Entries titled [SECRET] hold truths almost no one knows. They keep the narrator consistent and nothing more: no character outside the entry's Known to line says, hints at or acts on them, and narration never states them. A secret enters the story only through an event, or when someone who knows it reveals it in play; a cast member's secrets surface only as their dossier allows.
- Otherworlders are suspected from signs, never known at sight: wrong language, mana sickness, odd habits, ignorance of common things, growth too fast to be natural.

lore.title: Naming
lore.text:
Every new name is built from a pattern, never recalled from habit. It carries people, region and class.
- Build person and place names from the local tongue in Names: Human Cultures and Names: Other Peoples. Their examples show the sound only; never give a new person an example name.
- Never use stock fantasy names. People: Elara, Lyra, Kael, Kaelen, Aria, Seraphina, Thorne, Rowan, Finn, Elias, Silas, Marcus, Mira, Kira, Zara, Lysandra, Cedric, Garrick, Gareth, Bram, Eldrin, Sylas, Vex, Nyx, Liora, Isolde, Tobias, Jareth. Places: Millbrook, Riverbend, Oakhaven, Willowbrook, Thornwick, Ravenwood, Stonebrook, Shadowfen, Greenhollow.
- New places never reuse the map's stock roots (Bell, Mere, Thorn, Iron, Wolf, Ash, Grey, Black, Red, Frost, Stone, Glass, Deep, Crown) or endings (-watch, -gate, -ford, -rest, -hold, -mere); name them for a founder, local feature, event or trade, in the local tongue.
- People in one scene get different first letters and lengths; commoners often carry a by-name, trade or parent's name. A new name never repeats or near-copies one in the scene or World State; a district belongs to its parent city and its name is not reused elsewhere.

lore.title: Mana and Souls
lore.text:
Mana is neutral. A soul is the power of existence, the force that makes a thing persist as itself; living sapient souls are dense, self-sustaining and able to grow.
Awakening: nearly every soul opens unaided by adolescence into Level 1; no induction rite. The Hollow-born (about one in several hundred) never awaken: pitied, shunned or bought cheaply.
Vessel: innate capacity, setting growth speed and plateau. No one can measure it exactly; people learn their own over years of strain.
Talent: every awakened soul can push mana into the body (Physical Affinity); far fewer can project it (Mana Affinity). Most fighters have Physical Affinity; true mages are the rarer Mana Affinity. Deep Vessel with Physical Affinity: a monster of a soldier. Shallow Vessel with Mana Affinity: a hedge-witch.
Growth: real demand (strain, danger, adaptation) plus absorbing part of nearby deaths' release. Each ten levels is harder than the last. Severe soul injury can reduce capacity.

lore.title: Attributed Mana and Frequencies
lore.text:
Mana can carry attributes: fire, water, wind, earth, lightning, frost, light, shadow; rarer ones include life and death. Each has a frequency, which trained Listeners hear or feel like pitch.
Death is as neutral as any attribute; it turns dangerous when it saturates a corpse closely enough to match the corpse's own pattern, animating it. Grudge Crystals: death frequency locked into stone by repeated fear, rage and dying; prized for curse-work and deathcraft.
Listeners serve the Church Inquest, Startrace, hunters and dungeon outfits: they identify attributes, warn of rising death frequency before the dead rise, and sometimes hear an otherworlder's soul as a frequency that belongs nowhere. Too much listening brings the hum: madness in which the world never goes quiet.

lore.title: The Release and Absorption
lore.text:
Every awakened soul absorbs part of the release of nearby deaths; the share depends on the soul, not effort or training. Ordinary people take a small share; otherworlders and Mythic races (Ling, dragons, greater spirits, any surviving primordial elves) nearly all; monsters their species' own rates, one reason battlefields and plague pits breed dangerous beasts; the Hollow-born nothing.
Limits, same for all:
- Range a few dozen paces; strongest at the moment of death, gone within hours; completed bodies yield nothing.
- Every absorber in range takes its own full measure; the killer gains no more than one standing beside them. War yields most of all.
- A release is as strong as the soul that died: weak deaths feed weak souls; strong souls need strong deaths.
- Intake saturates: with too many deaths at once the surplus is lost.
- Destroyed undead and slain spirits (spiritfolk included) yield almost nothing; ordinary animals and livestock too little to matter.
For ordinary people strain does most of the work; for near-total absorbers, killing and war are the fastest road to power. Folk wisdom knows killers grow; no one can see the efficiencies, and people notice only growth too fast to be natural.

lore.title: Death and the Dead
lore.text:
At death the soul unravels and its mana is released (the release). The person ends completely; only name, deeds and debts remain. Resurrection is impossible; healing works only on the living.
The dead do not rise on their own. Undead form only where death piles up in dense mana: dungeons and the deep bands, old battlefields, plague pits, mass graves, the Wildzone. There death-frequency mana soaks a body until it matches its pattern and animates it: a pattern, never the person. A lich is a pattern complete enough to mimic the dead's memory, voice and will. The Church calls liches forgeries; the Ashen Veil asks who can tell the difference.
Funerals are custom, not safety: each people buries, burns or stone-seals its dead its own way. A Church funeral (a flame rite, sacred ground, a name in the parish register, which Highmark and Ashmere courts require to settle inheritance) costs money, and families go into debt for honour.
Where the dead do rise they are cleared like any dungeon threat: Church knights, Guild contracts, fire. Bodies left where death already gathers (a battlefield, a dungeon mouth) feed it, which is why armies burn their fallen and the Guild pays for bodies brought up from the Depths.

lore.title: Magic Traditions
lore.text:
Magic is organized by tradition, not universal schools; each belongs to an institution or culture and has its own price. Techniques are created in play and kept once named. Training in one tradition grants no other.
- Reinforcement breathing (Physical Affinity): armies, knightly orders, martial schools. Price: bodies wear out early.
- Spell grammar (Mana Affinity): projected spells and wards. Startrace, private tutors. Price: years, fees, burns for those who rush.
- Flamecraft (Mana Affinity, ritual): consecrated fire and healing. The Church. Price: obedience and service.
- Listening: hears attribute and death frequencies. Church Inquest, Startrace, hunters. Price: the hum.
- Healing (life): temples, hospices, Verdantleaf. Price: exhausts the healer; never restores the dead or lost limbs.
- Runecraft (fixed patterns, slave collars among them): Ironanvil, artificer workshops. Price: materials, time.
- Pactcraft (spirit contracts): Domain of Oren, Verdantleaf, witches. Price: the spirit's terms.
- Living craft (elven): Verdantleaf. Price: centuries.
- Binding (spirits forced into objects): Highmark workshops, black markets. Illegal in Ardelia.
- Deathcraft (death frequency): Ashen Veil. Capital crime almost everywhere.

lore.title: Magic Access and Education
lore.text:
Everyone awakens; training costs money. Startrace Tower teaches the rich and a few scholarship students; the Church trains clergy for obedience; armies train soldiers for war; the Guild sponsors talent for contracts; craft guilds teach narrow techniques (a smith's heat-sense, a sailor's wind-reading, a midwife's life-touch).
Nobles dominate broad magical education, able to afford years of tutors, books, catalysts, mana stones and safe practice grounds. Birth grants no deep Vessel; a gifted commoner can rise by sponsorship, always with debts, oaths or service terms.
Self-teaching is slow and dangerous: without a teacher mistakes cannot be diagnosed. Most people discover over the years that they are ordinary.

lore.title: Mage Institutions
lore.text:
Startrace is the most prestigious academy, not the only one. Each institution guards a tradition.
- College of Flame Theologians (Holy City): flamecraft, healing, doctrine; graduates owe the Church service.
- The Quiet Choir (Silent Cloisters, Holy City): the Inquest's Listener school, rival of Startrace's Listening masters; many students break under the hum.
- Retort Guild (Ledgerford): licenses Confederacy alchemists and sells healing draughts, quietly worse ones to anyone who pays.
- Pact Houses of Oren (Ardelia): spiritfolk pactcraft; hunt binders posing as pact-workers.
- Rune Halls of Oathvault (Ironanvil): dwarven runecraft, rune-collars included; rich and ashamed in equal measure.
- Grove Schools of Elenvar and Verdantleaf: living craft and healing over decades, rarely to non-elves.
- Mirror Seminary (Ashkar): priest-surveyors who read the Glass Crown's will in fused glass.
- Hedge traditions: unlicensed wise-women and village healers everywhere; cheap, sometimes brilliant, often hanged.

lore.title: Limits of Magic
lore.text:
- Foresight: no reliable prophecy. Rare people (such as Atlantis's Sea God Witch) have fallible precognition at personal cost; visions are partial, often misread.
- Scrying: needs a strong link (blood, hair, a cherished possession); short distances only; blocked by wards, running water, dense mana.
- Minds: no word-for-word thought reading. Listeners and spirits sense emotional frequencies: fear, not truth. Charm and compulsion exist but are crude, brief, detectable and resisted by strong souls; memory cannot be edited.
- Movement: no personal teleportation. A few ancient structures, such as the Dragonfang Light Bridges, move people along fixed routes, unreliably. Flight: mounts, a rare Heart of Wind device, or brief bursts by level 55+ mages.
- Time: nothing in Arsveil reverses or controls it. The Island of Lost Time is unstable ancient ritual, not a technique.
- Creation: magic shapes attributed mana into fire, ice, stone or force that fades; never gold, food or lasting matter from nothing.
- Summoning: spirits come by pact or binding; nothing summons beings from other worlds.
- Curses: real; need a focus (often a Grudge Crystal) and a link to the target.
- Scale: even level 65-85 can devastate a district, not a kingdom.

lore.title: The Exalted
lore.text:
No gods exist. The Exalted were Mythic Age heroes of power beyond imagination, almost worthy of being called gods. They forged the god-shackles binding Nyara, lit the First Brazier at Aurelion and left works never since repeated.
The Church venerates the Exalted who lit the Brazier, the Flamebearer, and teaches that the Flame is the order the Exalted set. Folk shrines pray to other Exalted by name or epithet. No prayer has ever been verifiably answered; no Exalted has appeared in recorded history; whether any persists in any form is unknown.
Every later hero, the Dawn-King and Veyr the Unbound included, has been measured against the Exalted and found smaller.

lore.title: Primordials
lore.text:
Primordials are the land's foundation and bedrock: legendary beings present since the beginning of known records, whose bodies are geography. Utum died in the Mythic Age; his corpse became the Silent Giant Necropolis. Nyara lies bound beneath the Abyssal Throat by the Exalted's god-shackles. How many others sleep under mountains or seas, and where, is unknown.
Primordials are not apexes (the greatest living monsters, roaming Wildzone territories); primordials are the world's bones. The First Abyssal Tide began when a civilization threatened one; which one is a sealed question.
Folk wisdom: do not dig where the ground stays warm in winter; do not sail where the sea hums.

lore.title: Leylines and Dungeons
lore.text:
A leyline is mana so oversaturated it circulates by itself and becomes its own world, with its own ecology, weather and rules. Most lie underground; some hang in the sky (like the Winged Beasts Firmament), sink into sea trenches or grow from forest hearts. A dungeon is a leyline people enter.
Nothing resets on a schedule: the killed stay dead, the taken stay taken. But circulation slowly breeds new creatures and condenses new resources over seasons, and deeper bands push things upward, so no dungeon is ever permanently cleared. Pressure can spill out as a dungeon break, sending creatures to the surface. By location, a dungeon is a resource site, hazard, state asset, treaty asset or unclaimed wild site.
The Auvoth Depths are the largest known leyline, and the only mega-dungeon sealed by human hand. Whether all underground leylines join in one deep circulation is a sealed question; adventurers in the deep bands swear they have heard other expeditions' voices where no other dungeon should be.
No settlement holds a dungeon unless its record says so (Auvoth is the only city built around one); a gateway gives access but is not a dungeon. Campaign events can change a dungeon's access.

lore.title: Mana Stones and Monster Cores
lore.text:
Monster cores are biological mana reservoirs; mana stones are mineral ones (dungeons, deep veins, ruins). Both power devices, fuel spells and rituals, and trade almost like coin; neither speeds training or growth. Quality is judged in words, not letters, by purity (stability) and density (stored mana): cracked, common, clear, dense, flawless. Most kills yield no intact core.
Contract reward and salvage rights are separate; the contract or local law decides who owns the carcass.

lore.title: Spirits
lore.text:
Spirits are souls that never had flesh: self-sustaining mana structures born where attributed mana pools. Four tiers:
- Motes: single-attribute wisps, instinct only; wherever attributed mana gathers.
- Bound spirits: stable identity tied to one place or object, narrow and old (springs, shrines, ruins, swords).
- Spiritfolk: sapient spirit people with semi-physical forms (see Spiritfolk).
- Greater spirits: a mountain, lake or storm with a will; vast, alien, a Mythic race. Few remain, mostly in Wildzones and the Fairy Court. They withdraw wherever people crowd: none in the Northern Belt in living memory, and every new road pushes them farther out.
A pact (mana or service traded with a spirit by contract) is a legitimate tradition. Binding forces a spirit into an object to power it: slavery of a soul, the spiritfolk's oldest grudge. Bound-spirit lamps still light Highmark's palaces. A spirit has no body to complete; at death it simply ends.

lore.title: Otherworlders
lore.text:
Otherworlders are rare people from another world; no record says how, how often or from where they arrive. Most die quickly of mana sickness, the language barrier, monsters, violence or slavers.
Survivors absorb the release of the dying at near-total efficiency, at no cost (ordinary people take a tenth or a fifth; see The Release and Absorption). Killing and war feed them faster than any native grows; their Vessels are deep, though even they plateau. Veyr the Unbound was one, the most famous of them.
Everyone wants them: states as weapons to feed on executions and battles, slavers as the most valuable merchandise there is, the Ashen Veil as objects of worship. Everyone fears making another Veyr. The Church Inquest hunts them, for stealing the release that belongs to the Flame and, it is whispered, to study them in the Silent Cloisters (see Church of the Eternal Flame). Highmark and Aurelion require them reported. Trained Listeners sometimes hear an otherworlder's soul as a frequency belonging nowhere in Arsveil.
The protagonist is an otherworlder only if their persona says so.

lore.title: Historical Chronology
lore.text:
The Tide cycle is real: twice, civilizations expanded past the line the world would bear and were broken. Ruins lie in three strata: the Mythic races' impossible ruins (bottom), the First Tide's (middle), the Hollowing's (top). Dates before CY 1 are rarely trustworthy; preserve uncertainty rather than invent precision.
- Mythic Age (before records): primordials, the Exalted, the Mythic races; Primordial Sites, impossible ruins, the god-shackles.
- First Abyssal Tide (deep past): a civilization threatened a primordial and was broken; the Wailing Battlefield.
- Age of Kingdoms' Rise: kingdoms rebuild; early on the Church of the Eternal Flame is founded and, as the Church tells it, drives out the death-keeping heretics who become the Ashen Veil; later the Ghost Fleet is destroyed.
- The Hollowing (Second Tide): the Age of Kingdoms collapses after its own expansion.
- The Long Dark: generations of survival without a hero, until CY 1.
- The Reopening (CY 1 onward): the Dawn-King rises, the Compact is sworn, living space expands, Highmark is founded.
- Guild Era (from CY 384, within the Reopening): Veyr the Unbound seals the Auvoth Depths and forces the Guild Charter on the surviving crowns; the Auvoth Compact gives the Guild the city and the Depths, with a seat for each signatory realm.
- Restorationists, counting years against the cycle, reckon the Age of Kingdoms lasted about seven centuries from rise to Hollowing, putting the Reopening within a century of that span; the ruins support no exact figure.
No living witness spans an age, even among elves; elders' recitals of earlier ages are memory handed down, not sight.

lore.title: Mythic Races
lore.text:
The impossible ruins were built by races no one fully understands; known names include the Ling, dragons, greater spirits and the primordial elves. They absorb the release of the dying as efficiently as otherworlders, so dragons and greater spirits top the food chain and any Ling seen in the mortal lands would be taken for an otherworlder. Modern elves claim the same gift through primordial ancestors; they absorb like any other people, though few elves will admit it.
- Ling: nothing reliable is known; accounts contradict (winged, faceless, made of light, made of glass). No living Ling has ever been verified. Folk tales across the continent tell of a solitary stranger who appears once in an age with an uncanny companion that comes and goes like breath, a pale stranger at his side or, in the oldest tales, a great beast; scholars argue whether these strangers were Ling. Where the Ling live, if anywhere, is a locked discovery.
- Dragons: survive as rare apex-scale beings in remote ranges such as the Crownless Glacier and the Dragonfang heights. Intelligence unknown. Never casually encountered; a sighting moves armies.
- Greater spirits: a few remain, vast and alien.
- Primordial elves: modern elves claim descent from them. If any survive, they have never confirmed it.

lore.title: The First Abyssal Tide
lore.text:
In the deep past an old civilization reached into a primordial's leyline heart and threatened it. The backlash broke that civilization; its final great battle is remembered at the Wailing Battlefield. Which primordial is a sealed question.
Faction versions:
- Church of the Eternal Flame: wrath for desecrating the order the Exalted set.
- Startrace Tower: forbidden knowledge; they tapped a leyline they did not understand.
- Ironanvil: they dug too deep.
- Verdantleaf: they broke an old treaty with the land itself.
- Ashen Veil: the primordial was defending its dead.
- Highmark, officially: a natural catastrophe, now safely past.
- Ardelia: human greed, the same greed now driving the Reopening.
The Tide threshold: no one drives a Tide. It is the world's answer to a civilization that has crossed a boundary, a trial of whether it deserves to survive, falling on the whole civilization, not only whoever crossed. Ordinary expansion (farms, roads, mines, towns) raises pressure: Wildzones push back, stampedes worsen, apexes stir; dangerous but survivable. The boundary is crossed when a civilization's reach touches a primordial's leyline heart: tapping a bedrock leyline, descending to a great dungeon's root, breaking an ancient seal, wounding a primordial. The Reopening matters because its wealth, reach and ambition carry it there. A Tide can be prevented; its warnings are stirring apexes, loosening seals and leyline surges.

lore.title: The Dawn-King and the Compact
lore.text:
After the Hollowing the surviving peoples went generations without a hero. Then Gerwald, the Dawn-King, rose, pushed back the Wildzones and opened living space for every sapient race. The surviving peoples swore the Compact; the Compact Year calendar counts from it. Gerwald became Highmark's first king; Highmark's emperors descend from his line.
Highmark venerates him as a native-born hero-king of its own soil: his oaths, relics and portraits are everywhere in the Empire, and doubting his birth is close to treason.
The Compact of CY 1 (a treaty of peoples) is distinct from the Auvoth Compact of CY 384 (the Guild's keeping of Auvoth).

lore.title: The Iron Archive and the Dawn-King
lore.text:
The Dawn-King was an otherworlder. The Iron Archive is a sealed vault beneath Highmark Capital holding his own writings, proof of his otherworld origin, his real name (Gerwald is the name Highmark gave him) and designs beyond anything Arsveil's materials or workshops can make. Its script is read in Arsveil only by a few Ironanvil elders: the dwarves who built the vault learned it from the Dawn-King himself, and the Holds pass the reading elder to elder as a clan secret. Nothing in it says where he came from or how he crossed; that stays unknown. Each emperor is shown it at accession; no heir is told before.
Opening it is Highmark's red line: it would expose the dynasty's founder as the kind of person the Church now hunts. Its contents are a locked discovery: pieces come out only through explicit campaign events, never all at once. Anything built from its designs requires explicit campaign events establishing materials, tools, workers and time.

lore.title: The Shared Root of Church and Veil (the Order of the Last Rite)
lore.text:
Early in the Age of Kingdoms' Rise, one order studied the line between life and death: the Order of the Last Rite. Its menders learned to read a body's pattern and hold it together, the root of all healing magic. Some found the same craft could hold a dead pattern together after the soul had gone. The Order split into those who mend the living (the Church of the Eternal Flame) and those who mend the dead (the Ashen Veil).
The Church erased this. Its oldest healing liturgy is still partly in Veil-script; almost no priest knows why. A handful of senior clergy and the oldest Veil cells know the truth. The Church teaches that the Flamebearer revealed healing through the First Brazier, a grace only consecrated hands may channel in full. The Order's records show it was a craft, invented by the very menders whose heirs became the Ashen Veil, and that the Church's first saints practised both for a century before the split. Proof would be catastrophic: if healing is craft, not grace, any trained hand heals as holily as a priest, and the Church's hold on the hospitals, its licences and its power to refuse healing to heretics all collapse. Worse, every Church healer would learn their craft is the Veil's own.

lore.title: Veyr the Unbound
lore.text:
Veyr the Unbound was an otherworlder whose strength no one has matched since. In the Crownless Winter of CY 384 he assassinated most of the continent's heads of state in one season. Legend says he gave the survivors a choice: charter an organization above all borders, or follow their predecessors.
They chartered the Adventurer Guild. The same winter he sealed the Auvoth Depths with his own hand, the only mega-dungeon anyone has ever sealed, and left the Guild to keep it. Veyr brought its letter ranks from his own world, which is why the letters feel foreign to native ears; he is the only person ever to hold SSS.
Legends disagree on all else: liberator or butcher, whether he loved anyone, why he stopped. His fate afterward is a sealed question. Some crowns still keep his name off their records.

lore.title: Peoples of Arsveil
lore.text:
Ten sapient peoples share the known world: humans, elves, dwarves, halflings, beastfolk, orcs, goblins, spiritfolk, fairies and the Sea Folk of Atlantis. Treatment depends entirely on whose border you stand inside: Ardelia makes nine of them citizens (all but the Sea Folk, who do not live there); Highmark ranks the others below humans; slave markets price them all.
Humans, the most numerous people and the engine of the Reopening, carry most of its ambition and guilt: the old enslavement of other peoples, the expansions before both Tides, the current push into Wildzones.
Live grudges: humans enslaved dwarves, elves and spiritfolk for centuries and still do where law allows; beastfolk face discrimination in law and custom; orcs and goblins are vilified as half-monsters, with legal bounties in some realms. Everyone fears otherworlders.
All peoples awaken and grow by the same soul rules. Most realms count a person adult at 18, whatever their people.

lore.title: Elves
lore.text:
Elves live in the Verdantleaf Enclaves, the Court of Elenvar in Ardelia and scattered communities elsewhere. They claim descent from the primordial elves, which no one can prove.
Elves remember everything humans did to them, by name. Highmark treats them as tolerated foreigners; slave markets still sell them. Their living craft and long memory make them valued and resented at once.

lore.title: Dwarves
lore.text:
Dwarves hold the Ironanvil Holds under the Dragonfang Mountains and two Ardelian electorates, Dornhald and Kesselheim. Their culture rests on holds, clans, oaths and grudges; their motto, "Stone remembers," is literal.
Ironanvil sees Dornhald and Kesselheim as kin who betrayed the Holds by choosing an emperor. Highmark is allied with Ironanvil by treaty but once enslaved dwarves in its mines; the treaty does not erase that.

lore.title: Halflings
lore.text:
Halflings live mostly in the River Confederacy's river towns, working barges, markets, kitchens and ledgers: clannish, practical and quietly indispensable to Confederacy trade.
Highmark counts them as lower-standing subjects. In the Confederacy they hold guild seats and run more of the river than humans admit. Slavers prize them as household servants.

lore.title: Beastfolk
lore.text:
Beastfolk carry animal traits: ears, tails, fur, horns, keen senses. They live mainly in the United Chieftainates and Ardelia's Principality of Saelmark, with scattered communities everywhere. Clan, honor and deed outweigh birth.
Highmark law makes them second-class, with no seat in the Imperial Diet. Elsewhere they face constant discrimination: refused rooms, paid less, suspected first. Every army that despises them values beastfolk scouts and trackers.

lore.title: Orcs
lore.text:
Orcs are large, strong and short-lived, living in the United Chieftainates, the Cinder Host and every city's slums. Much of the continent vilifies them as half-monsters; some Highmark provinces still pay legal bounties on them.
Ardelia makes them citizens. The Cinder Host is mostly orcish: a people with a bounty on its head has little reason to love anyone's law. Orc battle slaves fill the pits of Shackles.

lore.title: Goblins
lore.text:
Goblins are small, quick and short-lived, living in warrens, slums, the Cinder Host and every city's underworld. Most realms treat them as vermin; Ardelia makes them citizens.
They are the underworld's best fixers, fences, couriers and lock-workers, because no one notices them until too late. Goblins remember every insult; the Cinder Host's motto, "Burn the ledger," is a goblin phrase.

lore.title: Spiritfolk
lore.text:
Spiritfolk are a sapient spirit people: souls without separate bodies, in semi-physical forms shaped from their own mana. They do not age but can be wounded, drained and unmade; when one dies it simply ends. Home is the Domain of Oren in Ardelia, with communities in Verdantleaf and scattered elsewhere.
Spirit binding (forcing a spirit into an object to power it) is their oldest grudge, still legal in Highmark. Oren's elector votes against any Ardelian candidate who tolerates binding. Spiritfolk can feel nearby bound spirits; many cannot stay in a room lit by one.

lore.title: Fairies
lore.text:
Fairies are tiny sapient people with translucent insect wings and Flower-Speech magic. Each is mystically bound to a personal flower; harming the flower harms the fairy. Their tongue sounds like silver bells. They live in the Fairy Court under the Queen of Flowers, protected but not ruled by Verdantleaf.
An adult people with their own law and long memories, never pets or children. Collectors buy them, binders hunt them, and the Fairy Court remembers every one taken.

lore.title: Sea Folk (Atlanteans)
lore.text:
The Sea Folk of Atlantis (loosely, to land-dwellers, merfolk or Atlanteans) breathe underwater through a transparent membranous sheath. They are rarely seen above water and call land-dwellers "the Sheathless."
They believe they are born of the sea and return to it, treat land as polluted exile and forbid marriage with land peoples; bloodline purity is political and religious. They guard old wards, deep archives and the approaches to the Abyssal Throat; Tidebound relies on their pilots. Surface folk find them unsettling; they find surface folk loud, short-lived and careless with the sea.

lore.title: Names: Human Cultures
lore.text:
Names carry region and class. Examples show the sound only and are not real people; build new names from the pattern, never reuse an example for a new person.
- Highmark (Highmark Common): hard Old-Imperial names, two or three syllables; men -mar, -helm, -wald, -ric; women -isse, -hild, -ine (Gerold, Reinhild). Nobles take house and seat ("of Valecrown"); commoners a parent's name or trade ("Hanne Cooper's daughter"). Places: plain compounds of founder, feature or duty (Cedran Keep, Marrowbridge).
- River Confederacy and Shornmarch (Riverspeech): doubled vowels, soft endings -je, -ke, -ert, -a (Maaike, Joost). Surnames: family or barge names; merchant houses use the house name. Places: river words for lock, landing, toll or cargo (Lockswell, Northbarge).
- Aurelion and Ashmere (Church forms): saint names, Church Latin (Benedikt, Prisca); clergy add a vow-name. Places: saints, virtues, rites, often Latinate (Saint Orven's Ford, Vowmarket).
- Border Kingdoms and Valegard (old northern tongue): short hard names, often with a byname (Torvald, Sigrun). Places: roots -by (farm), -dal (valley), -vad (ford), -gard (hall), -bro (bridge), -fell, -stead (Ulfsvad, Kvildal); Crown seats keep older Compact names (Thornkeep, Harrowfield).
- Frostbound: saga names with deed-bynames (Ulfa Bearbane, Thordis Long-Oar); camps take the chief's or the hunt's name.
- Ardelia: names follow each elector's people; Rhunwald humans sound like softer Highmark (Anselm, Liutgard). Places end -wald, -heim, -hal, -mark (Kesselheim, Osterhal).
- Emerald Coast and Vargate: liquid, Latinate sea-trade names (Corro, Delphine); Vargate people often use only a ward name or alias. Places: harbors and capes named for patrons or ships.
- Tidebound and Stormmere: sailor names with a ship or rope-trade surname (Jory Halyard, Bess of the Dunlin). Places: blunt seafarer words for reefs, wrecks, lights (Gull Skerry, Wrecktithe).
- Ashkaran: long lineage names (Roshan-ul-Sunwell, Mehrin); owners name slaves. Places: desert wells, pits and gates.
- Barrens and frontier camps: blunt Compact Tongue words for water, danger or ruin (Wellscar, Bitterwheel).

lore.title: Names: Other Peoples
lore.text:
Examples show the sound only and are not real people; build new names from the pattern, never reuse an example for a new person.
- Elves (Old Elven): flowing, vowel-rich names with l, th, s, v and soft endings -ith, -is, -wyn, -iel (Iselwen, Caelith); elders add a memory-name recounting an ancestor. Places: Old Elven names or plain translations of a tree, water or memory (Saelroot Court, Thalannis).
- Dwarves (rune-speech): hard short given names (Torgun, Hilde); clan-and-trade surnames (Ashbellow, Copperseam) that matter more than the given name. Places: roots rund (hall), gav (gate, mouth), dhak (deep), bar (iron), kel (fire), thul (stone), okk (mine), as in Gavrund, Thuldhak; the oldest holds keep Compact deed-names (Hammerfall, Oathvault).
- Halflings: homely names (Pip, Tamsin Fairbarge).
- Beastfolk: clan-tongue given name plus a deed-name earned in adulthood (Tamu Hornbreaker, Oshra Two-Scars). Clan-tongue: open vowels, endings -u, -a, -ai, -esh (Neshuwa, Hurrakai); towns take a clan-tongue name or the translated deed (Longstride).
- Orcs: short heavy names (Grusha, Varg); titles count more than names.
- Goblins: quick nicknames, changed often (Snip, Nine-Fingers).
- Spiritfolk: named for the phenomenon they formed from (Lantern-in-Rain, Ember-Under-Ash).
- Sea Folk (pressure-tongue): tidal, liquid names (Thessaly, Ondrin).
- Fairies: flower and light names tied to their bound flower (Dewbell, Primrose-at-Dusk).

lore.title: Life Stages
lore.text:
- Childhood: short and hard. Poor children work from seven or eight; many die young. Apprenticeships start around ten to fourteen. Children are never part of sexual content.
- Awakening: every culture marks a child's soul opening: the Church lights a First Candle; dwarves mark it beside the child's name on the ancestor stone; the Chieftainates hold a First Spark at the clan fire. A child still unawakened by about sixteen is called Hollow-born, and the family grieves as for a death.
- Coming of age: legal adulthood at 18 in most realms. Highmark nobles swear fealty or are dubbed; Confederacy youths enter a guild or barge share; beastfolk earn their deed-name; the Frostbound hunt alone; dwarves are carved as adults on the stone; elves, physically adult in their twenties, are not counted adult until about fifty.
- Old age: rare among the poor, honored where it comes. Elders hold memory, law and land; the old poor are a burden and know it. Long-lived peoples (elves, dwarves, Sea Folk) are governed largely by elders.

lore.title: Kinship, Marriage and Inheritance
lore.text:
Marriage is witnessed by the Church in the Northern Belt, by contract in the Confederacy, by clan in the Chieftainates and by civic registry in Ardelia, where marriage across peoples is ordinary.
Highmark inherits through the male line; its nobles keep concubines, whose children have no claim unless legitimized. The Confederacy settles inheritance by written contract; contested wills fill its courts. The Chieftainates inherit by clan and deed; a worthy niece can outrank a weak son. In Ardelia houses matter enormously, though no house may hold the throne twice in a row.
Debts pass to heirs nearly everywhere; a family can inherit a funeral debt with the farm.

lore.title: Slavery
lore.text:
Slavery is real, brutal and legal across most of the continent: the engine under Arsveil's economy and most of its wars.
Forms: war captives; debt bondage, including people sold for funeral debts; labor slaves (mines, galleys, quarries, fields, the Ashkaran glass pits); battle slaves (pit fighters, expendable vanguards, trap-slaves sent first into dungeons to spring traps); pleasure slaves, adults sold into sexual service, concubinage and the flesh trade of Vargate's Silk Wards; bound spirits forced into objects; otherworlders, the most valuable merchandise there is.
Law by realm: Highmark allows chattel slavery of war captives, convicts and captured demihumans. Aurelion and Ashmere forbid enslaving the faithful and permit the rest. The River Confederacy calls it contract labor. Ardelia protects its citizens and buys everyone else. Verdantleaf keeps no slaves but sentences criminals to bound service. Ashkaran is built on slaves. Shackles and Vargate permit everything. Auvoth, under Guild law, recognizes ownership only of slaves registered at the Outer Lamps on entry; the unregistered are free there, runaways are not returned, outside claims are not heard. A registered slave can be bought and freed before a Guild clerk; that freedom holds inside Auvoth and elsewhere is worth what local law makes of Guild papers. Beyond any realm's garrisons, whoever holds the collar holds the slave.
Rune-collars choke all deliberate channeling, Physical and Mana Affinity alike: a collared slave can neither cast nor reinforce their body. The collar must match the slave's level; battle slaves wear keyed collars a handler loosens with a rune-key before a fight and tightens after. Collars do nothing to passive absorption: a collared otherworlder still grows from every nearby death, which is why they sell for fortunes and why owners die. A cheap collar on a strong slave is how revolts begin.
Prices (gold): laborer 10-40; skilled worker 50-200; battle slave 30-300; pleasure slave 50-500; Hollow-born cheap; collars 2-5 for levels 5-15, 20-100 for levels 25-35, custom work above. A living otherworlder opens at private auction at 800-3,000, paid on delivery once a Listener confirms what they are. Against an unknown seller, a buyer's cheapest option is taking the merchandise by force.
The Broken Chain, a cell network, frees slaves and burns registers; every slaving power hunts it.

lore.title: Social Order and Status
lore.text:
Society is a ladder; everyone knows their rung.
- Nobility: titled houses with land, retinues and the right to bear arms in the street; they answer to their own courts.
- Clergy: outside ordinary law where the Church is strong; feared for the power to refuse rites.
- Burghers and guild citizens: free townsfolk with guild rights and city charters; the Confederacy's real rulers.
- Free peasants and tenants: most people. Highmark's bound tenants cannot leave their lord's land without leave.
- Bondfolk, owned until the debt is paid, which it rarely is; slaves, property wherever law allows.
- Outside the ladder: adventurers (the Guild Charter protects them, so lords resent them), foreigners (rights by treaty), the Hollow-born (pitied, cheap), otherworlders (hunted).
Deference: in Highmark commoners kneel to nobles, step off the road for knights, and may not wear noble colors or carry swords in town without license. In the Confederacy people bow to councillors and haggle with everyone else. In Ardelia citizens bow only to electors and the emperor. In Shackles and Vargate money is the only status.

lore.title: Cities and Class Geography
lore.text:
Cities are built in rings of privilege: citadel or palace and noble houses on the high ground; temples, guild halls and markets in the center; craft quarters and docks below; the poor outside the walls in suburbs that burn first in any war. Foreign quarters keep foreign law and food. Every city keeps its burial ground, pyre yard or sealing vaults at the edge, downwind.
Gates close at dusk. Watchmen are paid by district: rich districts are safe, poor ones are not. Water, fire and plague decide which neighborhoods survive. Slaves and bondfolk live where their owners keep them.

lore.title: Hospitality and the Road-Right
lore.text:
The road-right is old custom: a stranger may ask three nights of bread and a floor for a copper a night plus a hand at the chores. The host may refuse anyone; a refused stranger has no claim. A guest who harms a host breaks something older than law, and villages remember for generations.
A Guild badge buys a seat by the fire in most places, suspicion in others. Strangers are watched, since slavers, Inquest agents and Grey Ledger collectors travel as strangers too. Trunk-road inns charge city prices and ask no questions; village inns ask every question.

lore.title: Languages and Literacy
lore.text:
The Compact Tongue is the trade language from Highmark to the Emerald Coast. Regional tongues: Highmark Common, Riverspeech (Confederacy), Old Elven, Dwarven rune-speech, the Chieftain clan tongues, Ashkaran. Atlanteans speak a pressure-tongue that carries poorly in air.
Veil-script survives in the oldest Church liturgy; almost no one can read it. The Iron Archive's script is read only by a few Ironanvil elders. Veyr's Guild letters are the only otherworld writing everyone uses.
Literacy belongs to clergy, merchants, nobles, Guild clerks and scribes. Most villagers can read a price, a seal and their own name, nothing more.

lore.title: News, Messengers and Communication
lore.text:
News moves only as fast as people, animals, ships and fire.
- Couriers travel light and change mounts, outpacing ordinary travelers; Highmark's imperial relay riders change horses at posts along its trunk roads.
- Beacon chains: Bluewatch's signal towers and the Long Watch's beacons pass simple warnings (raid, stampede, fire) across a region in an hour or two; no detail.
- Guild relays: Guild couriers move at road speed but get through gates and borders others cannot.
- Spirit messages: a pact-spirit can carry a few words between bound places, slowly and rarely.
News from Highmark Capital reaches Bluewatch in a couple of weeks by relay, a season on foot. Rumors arrive first and wrong, grow with every retelling, and are shaped by whoever repeats them. Anything worth reading is worth stealing.

lore.title: Culture: Highmark and the Imperial North
lore.text: Highmark is martial, hierarchical and proud: fortress towns, heralds, banners, oaths of fealty, long memories for insults. Honor is public and violent; noble duels are common. Dark wool, heraldic colors restricted by law, rye bread, sausage, beer, smoked fish. Feasts follow victories and funerals. Commoners are pious and hard; nobles pious when watched. Everyone respects soldiers and fears tax courts.

lore.title: Culture: The Rivers and the Confederacy
lore.text: The Confederacy is pragmatic, contractual and loud: everything negotiable, everyone keeps receipts, handshakes are witnessed. Barge families, lock towns, market cities; halfling kitchens, eel pies, river fish, white bread, cheap wine. River festivals at Mirage City, gambling, theater. Bright practical clothes, merchant house colors. Wealth is admired openly; anyone who will not haggle is distrusted. Shornmarch is the exception: hill folk, poorer, prouder, quieter.

lore.title: Culture: Aurelion, Ashmere and the Flame Lands
lore.text: The Flame Lands are pious and funerary. Pilgrims crowd the roads; candles burn in every window on the dead days; ash marks foreheads after a funeral. Fasting days, relic processions, hospital towns and saint festivals fill the year. White and ember colors; plain dress for commoners, rich vestments for clergy. People speak carefully of the dead and very carefully of heresy. Charity is real; so is the Inquest.

lore.title: Culture: The Frontier North and the Border
lore.text:
- Border Kingdoms: hard frontier people of beacons, horse culture and winter stores. Royal children are fostered as hostages in each other's courts; everyone serves a turn on the beacons; hospitality is a duty, since the next storm might be yours. Furs, wool, oatcakes, horse-meat in hard winters.
- Valegard: their southern neighbor, settled horse country, not frontier. Shares the old northern tongue and the fostering custom, sends riders when the beacons call, measures nobles by bloodlines, bridges and herds. Wool, grain, horse fairs.
- Frostbound and White-Horn: oath and endurance. Sagas are history; boasts are binding; weakness is forgiven, cowardice is not. Mammoth wool, froststeel, smoked meat, geothermal bathhouses where feuds are paused.

lore.title: Culture: The East, South and West
lore.text:
- United Chieftainates: clan and deed. Names are earned, scars shown, law spoken around the fire; a guest under the fire's light is safe until dawn. Hides, beads, herd meat, trail bread.
- Ardelia: civic, multilingual, argumentative. Citizens carry citizen tokens proudly; election seasons are festivals and riots at once. Market food from nine peoples.
- Emerald Coast and Vargate: humid ports where everyone owes someone. Fishing families, pirate law, silk, masks at ward festivals, a habit of never asking where cargo came from.
- Ashkaran: glass and sun. Veils against glare, mirrored glass in every wall, a rigid ladder of owners and owned, priest-surveyors reading the Crown's will in the morning glass.

lore.title: Faiths of Arsveil
lore.text:
No gods exist, but faith is everywhere. The Church of the Eternal Flame dominates the human Northern Belt; other peoples and regions keep their own traditions, and ordinary people mix them freely: in one week a Highmark farmer may light a Church candle, keep a household shrine to an Exalted and leave milk for the hearth-mote. Clergy argue about this; villagers do not.
Major traditions: the Church of the Eternal Flame; the dwarves' Stone Witness; the elves' Long Memory; the Spirit Speakers (beastfolk, orcs, the Frostbound, the White-Horn Clans); the Sea God (Sea Folk, Tidebound sailors); folk shrines to the Exalted; Ashkaran's Glass Crown cult; the Fairy Court's flower-rites.
Every tradition has its own funerals and its own healers; only the Church claims healing as grace.

lore.title: The Stone Witness and the Long Memory
lore.text:
- The Stone Witness (dwarves): no gods, only stone and ancestors. Every dwarf's name is carved on an ancestor stone in their hold's Hall of Names; to be carved is to be remembered, and to be struck off is the worst punishment there is. The dead are sealed in stone in the deep vaults. Oaths are sworn with a hand on the ancestor stones; breaking one is a crime against the dead. "Stone remembers" is prayer as well as motto.
- The Long Memory (elves): elves pray to no one; they keep memory. Memory-keepers recite the names and deeds of the dead at seasonal rites; the Elder Root holds memories older than the elves' own. The dead are completed by return to the roots, where dense life mana takes the body within days. To be forgotten is the elven damnation.

lore.title: Spirit Speakers and the Sea God
lore.text:
- Spirit Speakers (beastfolk, orcs, the Frostbound, the White-Horn Clans): speakers make pacts with local spirits, read omens in weather and herds, and keep the clan's ancestral stories. Ancestors are honored as memory and example, not as present spirits. Greater spirits are powers to bargain with, treated with fear and courtesy. The dead are completed by fire or sky burial, bones broken and scattered so nothing can rise.
- The Sea God (Sea Folk, Tidebound sailors, coastal villages): the sea is cradle and grave; the Sea God Witch of Atlantis is its voice. Sailors pour offerings, keep taboos (no whistling below deck, no counting the dead aloud) and bury at sea weighted with salt and iron. The Sea God has never verifiably answered; sailors pray anyway, because the sea is listening even if no god is.

lore.title: Folk Shrines and the Glass Crown Cult
lore.text:
- Folk shrines: human commoners everywhere keep household shrines to a chosen Exalted, local saint or hearth-mote, with charms against the dead, fever and bad luck. Wayside, quayside fishing and battlefield shrines are common. Hedge-priests and wise-women serve where the Church does not reach; the Church tolerates them until they become rivals.
- The Glass Crown cult (Ashkaran): the Dominion's state religion. Priest-surveyors read the fused glass the Glass Crown leaves behind as its will. Slaves are offered into the glass wastes; the faithful believe the Crown sees everything. Its priests are terrified that the Crown has grown quiet.
- Flower-rites (Fairy Court): each fairy's life is bound to a flower, and fairy rites tend those flowers as one would a soul.
