lore.title: Compact Year Calendar
lore.text:
Arsveil uses the twelve ordinary months, January to December, at their usual lengths: February has 28 days and there are no leap years. Dates are written [day] [Month] CY [year], counted from the Compact of CY 1. The year turns at midwinter.
There are no named weekdays: people count days, market days and feast days.
The moon keeps its own 30-day cycle, not tied to the months: new moon, then full moon fifteen days later. The scene block shows the phase. On moonless nights the Ghost Fleet rises and the Wailing Battlefield fights.

lore.title: Seasons and the Ordinary Year
lore.text:
- Spring (March to May): planting, tax assessment and the thaw, when winter's dead can at last be buried.
- Summer (June to August): campaign season; armies march, raiders ride, monsters migrate.
- Autumn (September to November): harvest and levy musters.
- The Turning (as winter sets in, from December): stampede season; Wildzone herds, the mammoth above all, migrate south ahead of the deep cold, and frontier villages watch their signal towers.
- Winter (December to February): hunger, Wildzone pressure, bodies that freeze before they can be completed. Debts come due at the year's end, in December.
These are civil seasons; local climate decides actual weather. Ordinary weather stays plausible; mana-dense sites can break the patterns locally.

lore.title: Prices: Property and Rent
lore.text: Property passes by charter, lease, inheritance, guild right or feudal grant; where sale is allowed, a village cottage costs 100-300 gold and a productive estate 15,000-150,000. Land is worth its water, soil, tenants, mills, roads, walls and security; without enforceable title it is nearly worthless, and frontier land changes hands in blood as often as coin.

lore.title: Wages and Contract Rewards
lore.text:
Daily wages: farmhand 10-20 copper plus food; master craftsman 1-3 gold; caravan guard 6 silver to 1 gold 6 silver; bodyguard to 5 gold; top specialist 5-15 gold. Soldiers: levy 1-2 silver when paid, career soldier 2-4, man-at-arms 4-8; knight 1-3 gold plus retinue. At sea: deckhand 3-6 silver, captain 4-10 gold.
Poor clients pay below the going rate or not at all. Expenses come out of the reward.

lore.title: Banking, Assay and Debasement
lore.text:
Large payments need chests, guards and wagons. Assayers check weight and metal; clipped, foreign or suspect coin is discounted or refused. Counterfeiting is a hanging offense.
Mints: Coinwater (Confederacy coin); Crown Mint in Highmark Capital (imperial); Osterhal (Ardelian); the Molten Core (dwarven silver, the continent's most trusted coin); Aurelion (Church silver for tithes and fees). Everyone else uses foreign coin. All mints keep the same weights on paper; Ledgerford's assayers discount any mint caught lightening its coin.
River Confederacy banks, centered in Ledgerford, issue paper notes redeemable in coin; the wealthy use them, villages and inns want metal. A note is only as good as its issuer and the distance to a branch that will honor it.
Debasement is a weapon: a crown that lightens its coin pays its soldiers today and loses its creditors tomorrow. In Shackles the Grey Ledger trades debts like grain; a debt can be sold to someone far worse than the original lender.
Debts pass to heirs. Unpaid debt ends in seizure, then bondage.
Highmark's silver is the continent's common coin: when Highmark clips it, prices rise everywhere it circulates, and assayers from Ledgerford to Shackles start weighing every coin.

lore.title: Trade Flows and Shortages
lore.text:
Each realm trades what it has for what it lacks: Highmark depends on Confederacy credit and Ironanvil steel; Ironanvil imports grain, timber, cloth and salt; Tidebound imports timber, iron and cloth; Atlantis needs surface metals; Ardelia ships highland grain, crafts and captives down the Belis River through Highmark's Barak Freeport; Ashkaran pays glass-steel for slaves; Shackles and Vargate move everything illegal.
Chokepoints: Barak Freeport, the Ledger River locks, Windcutter Pass, the Glass Road, the Long Passage. When one closes, prices jump within weeks and someone starts smuggling.
Markets: a settlement's speciality is regular, strong supply, never infinite stock. What a place cannot make or grow comes in by road or river: dearer, irregular, delivered to order or unavailable; a blocked route creates no replacement stock. Season, war, blockade, route closure and law change what is on sale; a district's market stays with its parent city.

lore.title: Taxes and State Finance
lore.text:
Commoners pay everyone; a peasant family typically loses a third or more of its harvest to rent, tithe and tax combined.
- Highmark: land tax, estate dues, Church tithe, road and bridge tolls, war levies in men and coin. Tax farmers buy collection rights and collect more. Nobles and clergy are largely exempt.
- River Confederacy: tolls, lock fees, customs, harbor dues, bank charges; light land taxes, heavy river taxes.
- Aurelion: tithe, pilgrim fees, burial fees. Ashmere: crown taxes plus tithe.
- Ardelia: imperial levies apportioned among the electors, each collecting its own way.
- The Guild: a cut of every contract. Shackles and Vargate: protection fees by ward.
States fund wars by debt, debasement and seizure. When a treasury runs dry, soldiers go unpaid, and unpaid soldiers take what they need.

lore.title: Law and Jurisdiction
lore.text:
Each realm's law runs inside its borders; frontier law is whatever the nearest garrison enforces. Nobles and clergy claim their own courts. Guild courts hear contract disputes everywhere and all law inside Auvoth. Foreigners have only the rights their treaties bought.
The Guild Charter adds three rights everywhere: adventurers under contract may cross borders; contract disputes go to Guild courts; no crown may press a registered adventurer into its army.
Gravest crimes: necromancy and deathcraft; failing to complete one's dead; harboring an unreported otherworlder (Highmark and Aurelion); spirit binding (Ardelia only); counterfeiting; desertion; theft of Guild salvage. Knowingly short-salting or not completing a burial: a fine per body, or the household head goes into bondage to pay it; if the dead rise and kill, whoever decided hangs.
Punishments are harsh and public: fines, stocks, flogging, branding, mutilation, enslavement, hanging; burning for necromancy where the Church rules. Debtors go into bondage, not prison: their labor is owned until the debt is paid, and where the realm allows, an unpaid bond is sold on as a slave. In Shackles and Vargate justice is private, priced and enforced by whoever owns the ward.

lore.title: Hunting Rights and Frontier Claims
lore.text:
- Game on noble land belongs to the lord. Poaching: flogged in the Confederacy, hanged in Highmark.
- Monster bounties, posted by lords, towns and the Guild, pay for proof of the kill; the carcass goes to whoever local law or the contract names.
- Wildzone concessions: the Confederacy sells frontier claim licenses for hunting, mining and salvage in its Wildzones; Highmark grants frontier fiefs, owing war levies, to anyone who can hold them; the Guild issues Depths permits by band in Auvoth.
- Unclaimed Wildzone belongs to whoever holds it. Claim jumping is common; frontier courts are slow, distant and bribable.
- Salvage default: contract first, local law second, finder last. Fights over carcasses are a leading cause of adventurer deaths after monsters themselves.
- Stampede carcasses belong to whoever's land they fall on; on unclaimed frontier, to whoever butchers and guards them first. Bluewatch's Watch-Captain claims a tenth of any butchered within a day's ride, for the River Council.

lore.title: Adventurer Guild
lore.text:
The Adventurer Guild was chartered in CY 384, the winter Veyr the Unbound ended the Crownless Winter and sealed the Auvoth Depths. Motto: "Contract above crown." Capital Auvoth, which it governs with a seat for every signatory realm; Guild Grand Hall in Sealcrown.
Charter rights everywhere, for members in good standing: adventurers under contract may cross borders; contract disputes go to Guild courts; no crown may press them into its army (the Guild's red line). Good standing: at least a year's membership, dues paid, contracts actually worked in the past year.
Registration never erases prior status (sworn soldiers, levied men, debtors, bondsmen, wanted criminals, unreported otherworlders keep theirs); members who register only to dodge levies are expelled. The Guild neither hunts nor reports otherworlders; it records the origin it is told. No crown or Church office may read its registers without a Guild court's order, though clerks sell copies and the Inquest pays clerks.
Enforcement: when a crown breaks the Charter, the Guild declares a Withdrawal: no contracts, monster work or dungeon salvage from Auvoth, and members leave the realm. Rival crowns back it. Highmark tried in CY 452 and gave in after one season of unanswered monster calls.
Letters, lowest first: F Registered, E Journeyman, D Proven, C Veteran, B Elite, A Paragon, S Legend. A contract usually pays, by letter: F 1-12 gold, E 8-30, D 30-120, C 120-600, B 600-3,600, A 3,600-20,000, S 20,000 and up; the Guild keeps its tenth to a fifth. Guild Rank certifies record, not power. Jobs above your letter are allowed at your own risk; the Guild will not pay to recover your corpse. A contract silent on salvage falls to the Guild's default, which splits it between party and client. Parties register with the hall before entering a dungeon (members, band, expected return); late parties are marked missing. No dungeon is ever permanently cleared.

lore.title: Who You Meet Where
lore.text:
- Northern Belt towns: mostly humans; halflings in river towns; dwarves in smithing and trade towns near the mountains; few elves; beastfolk as scouts, laborers and outcasts.
- Bluewatch and Shornmarch: humans, halfling barge crews, a few dwarven smiths, beastfolk scouts, and anyone passing through to Auvoth.
- Auvoth: every people, from every realm, in every condition.
- Aurelion and Ashmere: overwhelmingly human, with pilgrims from everywhere.
- Ardelia: genuinely mixed; each electorate leans toward its own people.
- Chieftainates: beastfolk and orc clans, with human traders.
- Western Barrens: humans, orcs and goblins, deserters, the Cinder Host.
- Emerald Coast and Vargate: humans, goblins, halflings, sailors of every people, rare Sea Folk, and slaves of every people.
- Ashkaran: humans rule; slaves of every people work.
- Verdantleaf: elves, with fairies in the Court. The north: Frostbound humans and White-Horn riders.
Individuals are never stereotypes of their people.

lore.title: Combat, Injury and Death
lore.text:
Combat is fast, ugly and often lethal: most fights end in seconds, and the wounded die afterward of blood loss, infection and cold. Lost limbs and eyes stay lost; no common healing restores them. Healing potions close wounds but leave weakness, scars and debt.
Level is not troop arithmetic. A stronger fighter dominates isolated foes but can still be surrounded, pinned, exhausted, netted or shot; formation, numbers, terrain, ambush, poison, fatigue and preparation decide fights as often as power. Gear improves protection and reach, never level.
With two known levels and nothing else intervening, the higher is stronger; protagonist status, fame or confidence never reverses that. Retreat, surrender, bargaining and flight are rational, and NPCs take them.
Strong Physical Affinity fighters (level 25 and above) can throw cutting pressure past a blade's edge: a feat of speed and reinforcement, not a spell, known among champions and veteran swordsmen.

lore.title: Martial Schools
lore.text:
Fighters learn in armies, orders and companies; the best learn in named schools with styles and rivals.
- Iron Guard Academy (Iron Guard Fortress, Highmark): officers and knights; formation, lance and heavy sword, reinforcement breathing drilled until the body breaks or holds.
- Duelling Houses of Mirage City (Confederacy): fencing houses selling lessons, champions and judicial duels; House Daubrey (single sword) and House Lisle (sword-and-dagger) have hated each other for a century.
- Pit Schools of Knifeglass Alley (Shackles): gladiator schools for slaves and the desperate; dirty, effective, lethal.
- Shield Halls of Hammerfall (Ironanvil): dwarven shieldwall and axe; oath-bound, unbreakable in tunnels.
- Hunt Lodges of Longstride (Chieftainates): tracking, ambush, spear, bow, monster lore; outsiders who survive the first hunt are admitted.
- Forge-Camps of the Frostbound: cold and endurance; each graduate forges their own froststeel blade.
- Snowbell Breath School (Kvildal, Dunmere): the north's purest reinforcement breathing; unarmored, slow to teach, terrifying in a fight.
- Guild drill yards (Auvoth, Sealcrown): practical dungeon work; cheap and full of the soon-dead.
Rivalries: Academy soldiers despise duelists; duelists mock soldiers; pit fighters kill both.
Otherworlder blade arts: a few small lineages of the katana, the draw-cut (iaijutsu) and the throwing spike (bo-shuriken), left by past otherworlders; rare, prized by duelists and collectors, and they draw the Inquest's attention to any practitioner.

lore.title: Armies and Warfare
lore.text:
Armies are pre-industrial, limited by food, fodder, roads, season and money. A great power fields a few thousand for an ordinary campaign, tens of thousands only for a war it cannot afford to lose. Most soldiers are level 5-15 levies; trained men-at-arms and knights reach levels 15-35; a level 45-55 champion can decide a battle but cannot hold a province.
Warfare: raids, sieges, frontier skirmishes, limited wars over a pass or river, and the sack of whatever cannot be defended. Battle slaves fill the front ranks of Ashkaran and some Highmark frontier units. Mercenaries, knightly orders and the Bloodbound League fill gaps levies cannot.
Every war feeds the release of thousands of dead, which the Church must complete and the Ashen Veil wants to harvest. An otherworlder on a battlefield grows stronger with every death around them, and every general knows it.

lore.title: Disease, Plague and Medicine
lore.text:
Disease kills more people than monsters do.
- Common: fevers, flux, winter cough, pox, wound rot, childbed fever. Most children in poor villages die young; childbirth is dangerous everywhere.
- Mana sickness: from overchanneling, deep dungeon bands or dense-mana sites; nausea, bleeding, collapse. Otherworlders often die of it soon after arriving.
- Death-blight: spread by corpses left in death-frequency mana (battlefields, plague pits, dungeon mouths); the reason armies and plague towns burn their dead quickly.
- Plagues: outbreaks close cities. The Silver Mark enforces cordons, Church clergy burn the dead, and the poor are walled in first.
Medicine: herbs, surgery, cautery, prayer and, for those who can pay, healing magic, which closes wounds and purges poison but often fails against disease and can worsen fevers. Barber-surgeons and wise-women serve villages; physicians serve the rich.

lore.title: Alchemy
lore.text:
Alchemy is a craft, not spellcasting: it turns monster parts, plants, minerals and mana stones into remedies, poisons and preparations. Healing draughts and wound salves are its most important products; corpse-salts, a Veil preparation, keep the dead fresh for raising.
It needs a workshop, glassware, heat, time, clean reagents and skill; mistakes poison or burn the alchemist. Alchemist's fire burns; it propels nothing. Startrace, Ledgerford's alchemist guild and the Church's hospitals train alchemists. Aurelion licenses healing draughts and hangs anyone selling corpse-salts. Poisons are legal to own almost nowhere and sold almost everywhere.

lore.title: Technology and Artifice
lore.text:
Production is household, workshop, forge, mill, shipyard, monastery and estate scale, powered by muscle, water, wind and mana stones. Siege engines are mechanical: rams, trebuchets, ballistae.
Artifice is workshop-scale: clockwork locks, mana-stone lamps, wards, rune-locks, cooling boxes for salvage, slave collars and a few rare mana-stone-fed devices. Every device is handmade, expensive and repaired by specialists.
Otherworlder knowledge is knowledge only: knowing something can exist does not give Arsveil the materials, tools, skilled workers or time to make it. Anything beyond this ceiling enters only through explicit campaign events, such as the opening of the Iron Archive.

lore.title: Spatial Storage
lore.text:
Spatial storage (pouches, rings) is rare and costly. Small pouches belong to successful adventurers, wealthy merchants and officers; rings to noble heirs, high officials, great houses and major guilds.
They hold only nonliving matter: living or self-acting things, including active undead, are rejected; ordinary corpses are matter. Storage never replaces the wagons, ships, warehouses and porters that armies, cities and caravans depend on. Customs posts, courts, palaces and Auvoth's Outer Lamps can require storage to be declared, sealed or searched.
Displaying storage discourages petty thieves and attracts professional ones.

lore.title: Monsters, Wildzones and Ecological Grade
lore.text:
Monsters are part of Arsveil's ecology, not evil; conflict comes from territory, hunger, migration, dungeon breaks and the Reopening pushing farms into their ranges.
Danger rises outward from settled land through frontiers and Wildzone rims to deep Wildzones and apex ranges. The Turning, the stampede season as winter sets in, can bring EG6-7 events to frontier villages.
Ecological Grade always names its scope, from EG1 (minimal) through EG5 (can destroy a village) to EG10 (apex event, possibly impossible to defeat, only to divert or flee). A weak but explosively breeding swarm can outrank a strong solitary predator.
Great apexes are living monsters beyond classification, treated as EG10 in their range; intelligence, intent and nature unknown. An apex's range never proves it is present, aware or hostile. No one has killed an apex; armies divert, settlements move, the wise leave.

lore.title: Bestiary: How Monsters Work
lore.text:
Monsters are animals shaped by mana: they eat, breed, migrate, defend territory and avoid pain. Most avoid people unless hungry, cornered, guarding young, pushed by migration or drawn by blood. Dense mana makes them bigger, stranger and deadlier, so danger rises toward Wildzones and dungeons.
A few species are sapient or nearly so: harpy flocks, Stormcrown thunderbirds of the Dragonfang heights, some fen trolls, dragons. Whether they are monsters or peoples is a live legal argument; Ardelia recognizes some as persons, Highmark none.
EG never converts into level. A kill is also a salvage claim and possibly a fight. Defeated creatures do not respawn; empty territory refills slowly from neighbors. Individuals vary (young and starving lower; old, alpha or mana-fed higher) and stay consistent once established.
A bestiary in context never cues an encounter; encounters follow season, territory, hunger and migration, and most days bring ordinary animals, people or nothing. New species and local variants may be created in play, kept consistent once established. Most creatures carry no attribute; show one through description (frost on its breath, sparks in its hide). Never state grade, level or attribute in narration; characters know them only as hunters' lore and estimates.

lore.title: Balance of Power
lore.text:
Nine great powers, each strong in a different currency of power, so every encounter between them is a trade:
- Highmark Empire: armies, fortresses, bureaucracy.
- River Confederacy: credit, barges, trade law.
- Holy Dominion of Aurelion: legitimacy, funerals, literate clergy.
- Ironanvil Holds: metal, fortification, siegecraft.
- Tidebound Covenant: fleets, ports, convoys.
- Verdantleaf Enclaves: long memory, living craft, defensive magic.
- Atlantis: the deep sea, old wards, archives.
- Ardelian Empire: elective legitimacy, citizenship across peoples.
- Ashkaran Dominion: slave legions, glass-road caravans, worship of an apex.
Regional powers: Ashmere, Valegard, the Border Kingdoms, the United Chieftainates, the Frostbound Tribes, the Emerald Coast principalities. Strategic enclaves: Startrace, Auvoth (the Guild's city), Shackles, Vargate, the Fairy Court, the White-Horn Clans. Transnational institutions: the Church, the Guild, the Wallwright League, the Silver Mark, the Bloodbound League, the Deepwalkers. Covert networks: Nightingale, the Hand of Oblivion, the Ashen Veil, the Broken Chain. Mobile power: the Cinder Host.
No power can dominate the others outright. Wars are limited, alliances shift, and an individual's strength never replaces armies, money, legitimacy or supply.
The Western Barrens are a frontier, not a state; the Free Marches share no jurisdiction by default. Wallwright, Silver Mark, Deepwalker and Bloodbound holdings are administered or associated, not borders; their sovereignty is unresolved.

lore.title: Highmark Empire
lore.text:
The Highmark Empire, founded by the Dawn-King at CY 1, is a militarized feudal empire of knightly tradition, imperial bureaucracy, fortress infrastructure, estate taxation and constant expansionist pressure. Motto: "The wall holds."
Rule: the Emperor, supreme sovereign and commander, rules through the Imperial Diet of great nobles, the War Office, tax courts, frontier governors and imperial clergy. Succession: the Dawn-King's male line by male preference; sons before daughters, but an emperor's daughter before his nephews. The founding charter's "through the Dawn-King's male line" can also be read as male heirs only, and the Diet must ratify every new emperor. The Diet, the army and the Church together settle contested successions.
Barak Freeport is Highmark-sovereign; "Freeport" is a name, not independence. Auvoth and Bluewatch are not Highmark.
Bleeds for: its founding myth of a native-born hero-king. Red line: anyone opening the Iron Archive. Needs: Confederacy credit, Ironanvil steel. Fears: Ardelian ideas, a new otherworlder.
Law: chattel slavery of war captives, convicts and captured demihumans; beastfolk are second-class; only humans sit in the Diet.

lore.title: River Confederacy
lore.text:
The River Confederacy is a river civilization of trade, contract law, canal engineering and merchant autonomy. Motto: "Water carries coin farther than banners."
Rule: the River Council of city delegates, guild magnates, river admirals, lockmasters, toll judges, chartered merchant houses and recognized territorial rulers. No one holds permanent command; emergency powers are negotiated, usually late. Thousand Sails is the principal council seat, Ledgerford the banking city; Coinwater mints the coin.
Members include the semi-autonomous Duchy of Shornmarch. Bluewatch is Council territory under a Watch-Captain, not a member.
Bleeds for: open rivers and honored contracts. Red line: a blockade of the locks. Needs: peace on the rivers. Fears: a Highmark default, since it holds a mountain of Highmark debt.
Law: chattel slavery is illegal on paper; debt bondage is legal, called contract labor. Halflings hold real guild power here. Licensed healing draughts are a Confederacy monopoly in all but name, and the Council taxes every sack.

lore.title: Duchy of Shornmarch
lore.text:
The Duchy of Shornmarch is a semi-autonomous frontier duchy within the River Confederacy, with a seat on the River Council. Shorn is its ducal capital and principal bastion. The duke governs local levies, forts, land law and frontier defense.
Bastion country: winter roads, hill farms, signal posts and forts facing the northern Wildzones and the approaches to Auvoth. Its villages are poor, proud and used to burying their own.
Bleeds for: its hill villages. Red line: Confederacy clerks trading its levies away. Needs: Council money for its forts. Fears: the Turning, and Highmark troops on the Auvoth road.

lore.title: Holy Dominion of Aurelion
lore.text:
The Holy Dominion of Aurelion is the territorial state of the Church of the Eternal Flame, built around the Holy City and the First Brazier lit by the Flamebearer. Motto: "Let nothing rise."
Rule: the High Pontiff, supreme spiritual leader of the Church and temporal sovereign of the Dominion, rules with the Conclave of Embers and a Dominion Chancellor who runs taxes, courts and granaries.
Strength: legitimacy. It crowns kings, sends or withholds healers, names heretics and refuses rites. Its electoral vote through Varden gives it a voice in Ardelia.
Bleeds for: its hospitals. Red line: open necromancy. Needs: kings who let only its healers practise. Fears: lay healers and heretics who say healing needs no priest.
Factions: Restorationists fear the Tide cycle and oppose expansion; Expansionists bless the Reopening.

lore.title: Church of the Eternal Flame
lore.text:
The Church of the Eternal Flame is the Northern Belt's most powerful organized faith, because it heals. Doctrine: the Flame is the order the Exalted set; life is a borrowed spark and healing tends it; the dead are done, and keeping them is theft from the Flame.
Its hospitals, infirmaries and hospital towns hold the best healers anywhere, and most trained healers are its clergy or owe it service. Every king needs it for his wounded and every city for its plagues. That is its power: it can send healers or withhold them, from rulers, from towns and from heretics.
Absolute in Aurelion, decisive in Ashmere, strong in Highmark, elsewhere dependent on faith and treaty. It blesses rulers, names saints, declares heresy and calls crusades.
The Church Inquest hunts necromancers, Veil cells and otherworlders. Doctrine calls the small share of the release everyone takes grace, and taking all of it theft from the Flame, so the Inquest hunts anyone who absorbs too well, otherworlders above all. The real fear is older: Veyr was an otherworlder, and the High Pontiff of CY 384 died in the Crownless Winter; the Church will not let power grow outside its reach again. It wants otherworlders alive: captives go to the Silent Cloisters and few are seen again; what is done to them there is whispered, never admitted.
Outside Aurelion, Ashmere and Highmark the Inquest is investigative only: it questions, watches, hires Listeners and pays informers. It cannot arrest, seize or punish in the River Confederacy, Auvoth or elsewhere; it must persuade local authority, buy cooperation, or wait for its quarry to cross into a realm where it can act.
The Church is not universal: other peoples keep their own healers and rites, and village herbwives and lay healers work everywhere. The Church tolerates them, licenses some, and watches any who heal too well.

lore.title: Kingdom of Ashmere
lore.text:
The Kingdom of Ashmere is a hereditary kingdom and the Church's closest secular ally, not part of Aurelion and not ruled by the High Pontiff. Motto: "By flame and law."
The Crown rules through flame-banner nobles, provincial courts and a royal council where senior clergy hold influential seats. The Church shapes coronation, burial law, education, charity and marriage.
Economy: grain, candle and relic craft, pilgrim traffic, hospital towns, funerary services. Ashmere completes more dead per head than anywhere else; its funerary trade is rich.
Bleeds for: its crown's sacred legitimacy. Red line: necromancy within its borders. Tension: royal law and Church doctrine keep colliding over who judges mixed cases.

lore.title: Duchy of Valegard
lore.text:
The Duchy of Valegard is an independent hereditary duchy and buffer state between the Border Kingdoms (north) and the southern powers (Highmark, the Holy Dominion, the Silver Mark), with the Wallwright League west and the River Confederacy east. It has treaties with Highmark and the Border Kingdoms and is subject to neither.
The duke or duchess rules through cavalry estates, landed houses, bridge courts, tax granaries and fortress captains. Noble horse lines are political assets.
Strength: horses, wool, grain, fortified crossings, toll leverage and some of the Northern Belt's best cavalry. Valegard avoids long offensive wars that would ruin its herds and harvests.
Bleeds for: its herds and crossings. Red line: being spent in someone else's war. Fears: Highmark's succession war pulling it in.

lore.title: Border Kingdoms Alliance
lore.text:
The Border Kingdoms are a defensive alliance of four small sovereign kingdoms sharing warning systems, winter logistics, hostage treaties and levy obligations, with no single monarch: Thornvale (capital Thornkeep), Redspire, the Lake Kingdom of Dunmere and Harrowmark (seat Harrowfield).
Alliance musters may place troops under a temporary elected commander without transferring sovereignty. A council chair rotates among the four crowns.
Bleeds for: the warning chain that keeps all four alive. Red line: one kingdom abandoning another. Fears: Frostbound raids, the Turning, and being bought piecemeal by Highmark.

lore.title: Ironanvil Holds
lore.text:
The Ironanvil Holds are a network of dwarven clan holds under the Dragonfang Mountains, with no single crown. Motto: "Stone remembers."
Rule: each hold follows clan law and elders. The Council Beneath Stone meets for treaties, common defense, shared roads and dangerous depths, and elects a Thane-of-Thanes to speak for the Holds. Holds have no assigned clans; never infer which clan owns a hold.
Strength: mining, metallurgy, armor, fortress engineering, siegecraft, runecraft (including the rune-collars every slaver needs).
Bleeds for: the name of the Holds. Red line: a hold leaving. Needs: grain, timber, cloth and salt from outside. Fears: secession to Ardelia, and the Stone That Walks shifting their passes.
Dwarves remember being enslaved in Highmark's mines; the treaty with Highmark does not erase it.

lore.title: Verdantleaf Enclaves
lore.text:
The Verdantleaf Enclaves, the elven realm of the far south, are governed by consensus of the Council of Tree-Speakers: elders, druids, ritualists and memory-keepers. The Elder Root, its most ancient voice, speaks through chosen interpreters. Motto: "We were here before you. We will be here after."
The Fairy Court is a separate polity under elven protection.
Strength: long memory, living craft, healing and defensive magic. Mission: hold the forest as it is and enforce old treaties that shorter-lived rulers keep forgetting.
Bleeds for: the forest's boundary. Red line: new roads into Thornheart. Needs: no one, it claims. Fears: the Reopening reaching it. Law: no slaves, but criminals are sentenced to bound service.

lore.title: Fairy Court
lore.text:
The Fairy Court is a hidden fairy realm south of Verdantleaf and separate from it: giant canopy flora, suspended habitats, luminous plants, and nature-attributed mana dense enough to sicken outsiders who stay too long. The Queen of Flowers rules. The Rainbow Bridge, a fairy-made canopy bridge walked to Starwater Quay, links it to the elves; it sometimes fails.
Many greater spirits remain within its borders. The Southern Coil hunts the rainforest rivers around it; the Court keeps to the high canopy and wards its own waters. Fairies are hunted for collectors and binding, and they remember. A dead fairy's flower is burned with her, or the body rises small and wrong.
Troubles: collectors' agents work the canopy's edge, and a fairy who goes missing is remembered by name at Court.

lore.title: United Chieftainates
lore.text:
The United Chieftainates are an alliance of beastfolk and orc clans across eastern plains, mesas, forests and steppe, governed by the Chieftain Council of clan chiefs, war leaders, spirit speakers, elders and renowned scouts; member clans keep their own law. A High Chieftain speaks for the Council; Battle Cry City is the seat of the Council and the Grand Muster.
Grand Muster: in an existential threat, clans owe warriors, scouts, mounts and supplies to a temporary muster under negotiated command.
Strength: scouting, tracking, monster knowledge, courier networks, mobile warfare. Every army that despises beastfolk hires their scouts.
Bleeds for: clan honor. Red line: slavers on clan land. Fears: Vargate's slave ships working its coast.

lore.title: Frostbound Tribes
lore.text:
The Frostbound Tribes are a mobile confederation of the northern taiga, tundra and ice forests. "Northern Barbarians" is a foreign insult, not their name.
Strength legitimizes leadership, but Frostbound strength means surviving hardship, protecting followers, keeping oaths and succeeding in hunt or war, not just winning duels. A Frost Queen or King leads from a moving war-seat; the Winter Moot of chiefs, forge-masters, spirit speakers and oath-holders settles succession and existential policy; no single feat compels every clan.
Strength: hardened warbands, froststeel craft, geothermal valleys, mammoth routes, winter warfare. They raid south in bad winters, and winters are getting worse.
Bleeds for: their oaths. Red line: southerners settling their hunting grounds. Distinct from the White-Horn Clans.
They have no fixed places: halls and war camps move with the seasons. Svartalheim is a legendary Frost-Iron thronehold and seasonal war-seat, not a mapped city. No Frostbound city lies north of Auvoth; camps there are temporary or hidden.

lore.title: White-Horn Clans
lore.text:
The White-Horn Clans are a mobile mammoth-rider confederacy with no capital. Clan elders, herd-masters, spirit speakers and proven riders meet at Hornwake Camp, a moving council wherever the great herds allow.
Economy: mammoth wool and ivory under clan law, hides, cold-weather guides, sled transport, preserved meat and rescue contracts. Military: herd screens, heavy mammoth charges, winter ambushes. They avoid sieges and cannot hold land far from the herds.
They are distinct from the Frostbound Tribes. Long Thunder drives their herds, and they say it does so on purpose.
Hornwake Camp may pitch north of Auvoth; it is never a city.

lore.title: Tidebound Covenant
lore.text:
The Tidebound Covenant is a maritime league of sea-lords, fleet captains, harbor princes, island delegates and merchant admirals under the Tidal Council. Motto: "The sea takes its tithe." Abysswatch is council seat and naval command. The Stormmere Isles are an autonomous member realm, with capital and privateer court at Stormmere Haven; assign no other port to Stormmere without canon. Vortex Port and Blackmast are contested harbors under uneven Covenant control.
Strength: fleets, ports, convoys, pilots, salvage.
Bleeds for: the convoys. Red line: closure of the sea lanes. Needs: Atlantean pilots. Fears: a war at sea it cannot afford, and the Black Trawl.
Atlantis is a separate sovereign kingdom, not a Covenant member.

lore.title: Atlantis
lore.text:
Atlantis: sovereign deep-sea kingdom under a vast transparent dome lit and warmed by Sea-Light Stones; the dome is inherited ritual work kept by priestly and artisan knowledge, not reproducible. Motto: "The deep keeps its counsel."
Its Sea Folk breathe underwater through a transparent membranous sheath, call land-dwellers "the Sheathless", and believe they are born of the sea and return to it. Bloodline purity is political and religious; marriage with land peoples is forbidden.
Rule: conservative theocracy and nobility. The Sea God Witch is highest spiritual authority and the Sea God's royal proxy; the Tide-Archon chairs the governing council. The Sea God has never verifiably answered; the Witch's power is her own.
Strength: deep sea, old wards, deep archives, coral craft, Sea-Light work. Guards the approaches to the Abyssal Throat.
Bleeds for: its wards. Red line: anyone touching the Throat's rune slabs. Needs: surface metals. Fears: Nyara's release.
Troubles: the wards at the Abyssal Gate are old, and pilots talk of things in the trench lanes that the council will not discuss.

lore.title: Emerald Coast Principalities
lore.text:
Emerald Coast: a string of small coastal principalities between the Chieftainate shore and Tidebound waters: fishing ports, timber harbors, pirate-tolerant towns, ruled by harbor princes who survive by paying everyone. Marisk: fishing and timber. Corrowen: southern harbor, last port before the Long Passage.
Vargate dominates in practice: the principalities sell it water, timber and silence, and in return Vargate's slavers mostly raid elsewhere.
Troubles: smugglers run every cove; a harbor prince's peace lasts exactly as long as his payments.

lore.title: Vargate
lore.text:
Vargate: underworld harbor city on the Emerald Coast. Saying: every crown has a door in Vargate it publicly denies using. No single authority: a patchwork of wards, each owned by a ward-lord, merchant house, slave factor or foreign interest under a ward compact.
Trades: sea slaving, the Silk Wards' flesh trade, information, otherworlder brokerage, stolen cores, smuggled cargo, anything that floats. Its ships run the Long Passage round the southern cape to Ashkaran.
Patrons: Tidebound, Ardelia, Ashkaran (slaves, secrets). Weakness: any ward can be bought against another. The Ashen Veil keeps a tolerated temple ward here. Rules by doors; rival of Shackles.
Visitors notice: masks at ward festivals, warm wet air, doors with no signs. Locals complain: Shackles' caravan cartels, ward-lords selling each other out, Grey Ledger debt collectors appearing in wards that thought they were safe.

lore.title: Ardelian Empire
lore.text:
Ardelian Empire: elective composite empire in the southern highlands; capital Osterhal. Motto: "No crown twice."
Rule: nine electors choose an emperor for a fixed 18-year term; six votes needed; no house may supply two emperors in a row. Electors: Crown of Rhunwald (human kingdom), Court of Elenvar (elven), High Hold Dornhald and Hold-Principality Kesselheim (dwarf holds), Republic of Belisar (merchant republic), Principality of Saelmark (beastfolk), Domain of Oren (spiritfolk), Sacred Principality of Varden (temple state; votes as Aurelion instructs), and the Lesser Estates seat, whose delegate the minor estates choose by majority at Osterhal before each election, so it can be bought.
Blocs: Crown Bloc (Rhunwald, usually Belisar) wants a strong emperor, a standing army and terms with Highmark's generals; Particularists (Elenvar, Oren, Saelmark) defend electors' rights, local law, citizenship; Frontier Bloc (Dornhald, Kesselheim) wants forts and money for the mountain and Southmarch frontiers. Varden and the Lesser Estates swing; Belisar sells its vote.
Citizenship crosses peoples: the nine peoples of Osterhal (all but the Sea Folk, who do not live there) are equal citizens. Citizens cannot be enslaved; non-citizens can, and Ardelia buys war captives without embarrassment. Spirit binding is a crime.
Southmarch, west and south of the Barak Gulf, is a contested Highmark-Ardelia frontier with no settled sovereignty and no settled markets; traders and raiders meet at forts and camps.
Bleeds for: citizenship. Red line: a hereditary emperor. Needs: trade down the Belis River through Highmark's Barak Freeport. Fears: a Highmark march down the Southmarch Road. Patrols Nareth's edge; lets no one in.

lore.title: Ardelian Constitution
lore.text:
- Eligibility: any Ardelian citizen of ten years' standing, of any people. The ban on consecutive emperors binds the emperor's house (family), not the electorate: an electorate whose ruling house just reigned may nominate from another house, though it rarely has one worth nominating.
- Deadlock: if no candidate has six votes by the term's last day, the emperor steps down anyway and the Arch-Chancellor (chosen by the electors for life) rules as regent: no wars, no new levies, no land grants. Electors vote again each season; after a year without an emperor, five votes suffice.
- Membership: realms join by treaty, enter the Lesser Estates and vote through its seat. A new electoral seat needs all nine electors to agree (has happened once). With a tenth seat, seven votes would elect; six after a year without an emperor.
- Citizenship: birth to a citizen parent inside the empire; ten years of imperial or militia service; an elector's grant within its own domain; imperial decree. Elector registries issue citizen tokens. Anyone without one is presumed a non-citizen and can be sold; proving citizenship without a token is a court case, and slavers do not wait for courts.
- The Knights of the Last Day remove an emperor who overstays and guard the regent.

lore.title: Ashkaran Dominion
lore.text:
Ashkaran Dominion: beyond the western glass wastes; the only state that worships a living apex, believing the Glass Crown chose it. Motto: "The Crown sees."
Rule: the Glass Regent rules from Ashkar as the Glass Crown's steward, through priest-surveyors who read the glass and slave-lords who own the legions.
Strength: slave legions, glass-road caravans, glass-steel. Its slaves are fed into the Glass Pits at the wastes' edge, where fused glass is mined and the Crown kept content. Largest slave buyer on the continent, via Shackles' Glass Road caravans and Vargate's Long Passage ships.
Bleeds for: the Glass Crown's favor. Red line: anyone hunting the Glass Crown. Needs: slaves. Fears: the Glass Crown going silent.
To the Northern Belt it is half rumor: a distant, rich, cruel empire that pays in glass-steel and never sends anyone back.
Troubles: glass-storms off the wastes strip caravans to the bone, and things burrow under the glass roads.

lore.title: Startrace Tower
lore.text:
Startrace Tower: independent academy-city, the continent's most prestigious school of mana theory, spell grammar, ritual craft, dungeon ecology, ancient languages, healing theory and appraisal. Philosophy: "Knowledge without restraint becomes another dungeon." Led by an Archmaster and council of masters.
Nobles and wealthy houses dominate attendance; commoners enter by scholarship, sponsorship, Guild recommendation or exceptional examination, always with obligations attached.
Rumor says the Tower keeps old records it denies having, and that its masters study the release of the dying on condemned prisoners bought from Highmark; the Tower denies both. Its masters argue among themselves whether the Reopening repeats an old mistake. Bleeds for: its archives. Red line: any crown seizing the Tower. Fears: being forced to choose a side in Highmark's succession.
It is independent although it lies in the Western Barrens: no Barrens, Shackles, Bloodbound or neighboring crown jurisdiction reaches it.

lore.title: Shackles City
lore.text:
Shackles City: criminal-mercantile free city in the western interior: black market, debt-bondage hub, smuggling crossroads, refugee sink, mercenary nest, slave market. Not lawless: it enforces a narrow, brutal commercial order.
Law: the Codex of Shackles treats debt, ransom, collateral, witnessed exchange and signed contract as the only reliable law.
Powers: Ironhammer Brotherhood (mercenary labor, pit fights, caravan muscle, prisoner transport); Grey Ledger (black-market banking, debt registers, ransom brokerage, arbitration; sells debts as others sell grain); Veil Market (stolen cores, illegal maps, forged Guild badges, relic fragments, forbidden texts).
It survives because every rival prefers it compromised and neutral to owned by an enemy. Its caravans run the Glass Road to Ashkaran. Highmark uses it quietly for deniable work; the Bloodbound League brokers contracts through it. Rules by debt; rival of Vargate.
It sprawls across a warren of yards, quays and tunnels about 10 km across. Dustbell and Westchain Hold are affiliated settlements outside it, not districts. Visitors notice: collars everywhere, contracts nailed to doors, no one asking questions. Locals complain: the Cinder Host on the caravan roads, Vargate stealing the slave trade, debts sold to worse men.

lore.title: Wallwright League
lore.text:
Wallwright League: independent military order and fortress league headquartered at Wallwright Hall. Its council of senior captains, wallwrights, quartermasters and siege masters elects a First Marshal for limited terms.
Mission: build and hold walls, train garrisons, test siege defenses, protect strategic crossings for whoever pays its charter fees. Defensive by oath; never fights a war of conquest.
Its wallwrights also build cities' sealing vaults and pyre-yards; its plague contracts wall the dead in with the living. Every side in Highmark's succession wants its engineers.

lore.title: Order of the Silver Mark
lore.text:
Order of the Silver Mark: Church-aligned holy military order headquartered at Silvermark Commandery, ruled by a Grand Commander and chapter under its own chapter law.
Mission: guard pilgrims, escort relics, protect burial roads, investigate grave desecration, reinforce plague cordons, fight mass undeath. Hunts Ashen Veil cells across borders; first called when the dead rise in numbers.

lore.title: Deepwalkers
lore.text:
Deepwalkers: independent underground charter league of surveyors, miners, rescue crews, tunnel guards, archivists and underground ferrymen. The Map Council at Deepwalker Hall validates routes, seals dangerous passages, assigns rescue duties and arbitrates claims by witnessed charts and marker stones.
Mission: map old roads, keep shafts safe, recover trapped crews, detect collapses, stop crowns or smugglers opening sealed depths. They swear the underground leylines connect and refuse to say what they have heard down there.
They bring their dead up from any depth and seal them in Lanternshaft's stone; a crew that leaves a body below is struck from the Map Council's rolls.
Troubles: tunnel collapses come without warning, and crews swear the deep passages shift.

lore.title: Bloodbound League
lore.text:
Bloodbound League: mercenary league and contract confederation centered on Bloodbound Camp-City; the name means witnessed blood-oaths and death-pay obligations, not blood magic. Governed by company captains, paymasters, veteran delegates and neutral contract judges.
Law: a dead soldier's share goes to his named kin; stealing it unites companies that otherwise hate each other. Motto: "Paid in blood, paid in full."
Sovereignty deliberately unresolved: no crown recognizes it, none can remove it. Brokers contracts through Shackles.

lore.title: Nightingale
lore.text:
Nightingale: artist-like thieves' network. Creed: "Wealth only gains meaning when it is in motion." Members call themselves redistributors and couriers of secrets, and despise crude robbery and needless murder.
A secret Nightingale King or Queen leads core specialists (theft, locks, disguise, infiltration, intelligence), with contacts in every city for fencing, safe lodging and information. Its hidden sanctum, the Nest, is compartmentalized; its center is believed to be in Vargate, with old roots in Shackles.
Three Non-Thefts: do not steal from the destitute; do not kill innocents except in extreme danger; do not prey on fellow thieves. Traitors are stripped, exiled and marked across every cooperating black market.
Oldest rule: never rob the dead; grave-goods are the one theft its fences will not touch.

lore.title: Hand of Oblivion
lore.text:
Hand of Oblivion: decentralized contract-assassin network, no headquarters. Creed: "We are everywhere. We are everything." It is intimidation, not omniscience.
Brokers carry contracts via dead drops, ciphers and disguises; independent Executors choose whether to accept. The "First Executor" is more symbol than ruler. Silent Sanctums: anonymous safehouses that move.
Anyone can be proposed as a target; not every contract is feasible, affordable or accepted, and protected targets cost fortunes. The Hand honors every contract it accepts, even from both sides of the same war.

lore.title: Ashen Veil
lore.text:
Ashen Veil: loose network of heretical cells, necromancers, corpse smugglers and plague scavengers; no state, no single ruler.
Belief: the menders' craft should not stop at death. Their necromancy is healing turned on the dead: it holds a body's pattern together after the soul has gone, so the dead walk, serve and seem to remember. Cells disagree violently whether a lich is the person who died. They worship otherworlders as souls that devour the release.
Trade: forbidden texts, stolen remains, Grudge Crystals, corpse-salts, poisons, false burial papers, curse foci, and healing the Church refuses, at a price no one should pay. Buys corpses from Shackles and Vargate; keeps a tolerated temple ward in Vargate.
The oldest cells claim to hold something that would break Aurelion; the Church calls it a heretic's lie. They hate the Grey Walker, which stills the dead wherever it passes.

lore.title: Broken Chain
lore.text:
Broken Chain: cell network that frees slaves, forges free papers, smuggles runaways and burns slave registers. Cells do not know one another; each answers only to whoever recruited it.
Every slaving power hunts it; Shackles and Vargate both pay for its members' heads. Many of its fighters ended up in the Cinder Host. Ardelia quietly tolerates it when it frees Ardelian citizens and hangs it when it frees anyone else.

lore.title: Cinder Host
lore.text:
Cinder Host: campaign-host with no capital: orcs, goblins, beastfolk, runaway slaves and deserters moving through the Western Barrens, led by a Warmother chosen in war. Motto: "Burn the ledger."
It feeds on war, raiding caravans and border forts; frees slaves it takes, enslaves no one, burns every debt register and title deed it finds.
Bleeds for: each other. Red line: chains. Needs: plunder. Fears: a real army turning west against it. To the Northern Belt a horde; to its members, the only place their lives have been their own.
It roams the Western Barrens, raids the Glass Road and Barrens towns, and presses Highmark's western border fortress at Ravenholt.

lore.title: Knightly Orders
lore.text: Seven knightly orders fight across the Northern Belt and Ardelia, each with a patron, motto and red line: the Wardens of the Last Wall (Highmark), the Knights of the Flame Banner (Ashmere), the Order of the Running Mare (Valegard), the Knights of the Last Day (Ardelia), the Long Watch (Border Kingdoms), the Order of the Sealwardens (Auvoth) and the Marchriders (Highmark's southern frontier). The Order of the Silver Mark and the Wallwright League are larger institutions.

lore.title: Wardens of the Last Wall
lore.text: Highmark's oldest knightly order, founded by the Dawn-King to garrison the roads toward the mountains and the north; based at Thornwall Redoubt on Highmark's northern march, where the roads from the Border Kingdoms and Valegard meet; the Last Wall's old earthworks run east and west from it, the line Highmark falls back to when the north is lost. Motto: "Until the last stone." Bleeds for: the Dawn-King's blood. Red line: kneeling to a ruler not of his line, so they oppose any elected emperor and any general's crown. Heavy infantry and knights, levels 15-35, a few champions. Proud, poor, old-fashioned.

lore.title: Knights of the Flame Banner
lore.text: Ashmere's Church-aligned cavalry order, blessed at the First Brazier. Motto: "By flame and lance." Bleeds for: consecrated ground. Red line: necromancy left unanswered. They ride against Veil cells, risen dead and heretics, and burn what they kill. Their knights train in flamecraft as well as the lance.

lore.title: Order of the Running Mare
lore.text: Valegard's noble cavalry order, drawn from the duchy's horse-lord houses. Motto: "First across, last to leave." Bleeds for: the herds and the crossings. Red line: being spent in someone else's offensive war. The best light cavalry in the Northern Belt, and the most expensive to hire.

lore.title: Knights of the Last Day
lore.text: Ardelia's order sworn to the electoral law, named for the last day of an emperor's term. Motto: "The term ends." Bleeds for: the 18-year term. Red line: an emperor who overstays, whom they are sworn to arrest. They guard elections, electors and the count. Every Ardelian emperor fears them a little, which is the point.

lore.title: The Long Watch
lore.text: The Border Kingdoms' shared order of winter wardens, under an elected commander. Motto: "We hold the cold." Bleeds for: the warning chain of beacons that keeps the four kingdoms alive. Red line: one kingdom abandoning another. Skilled in snow warfare, beacon signals and holding passes against Frostbound raids and the Turning.

lore.title: Order of the Sealwardens
lore.text:
The Guild's order in Auvoth, chartered under the Auvoth Compact to guard Veyr's seals and the Depths' gates. Motto: "Light at the seal." Bleeds for: the seals. Red line: anyone breaking a seal without the Seventh Seal Court's leave. They answer to no crown, come from every people, and are first to die in a breach, and know it.
Terms: one-year oath, 4-8 silver a day; recruits serve a month at the upper seals before any breach duty. All salvage taken on duty belongs to the Order. Deserters are hanged on the Seventh Seal Terrace under Guild law.

lore.title: The Marchriders
lore.text: A Highmark frontier order of mounted knights and sergeants on the Southmarch, based out of Stoneford. Motto: "We ride where the law ends." Bleeds for: their own garrisons and each other. Red line: being left unpaid while the capital feasts. Hard, brutal frontier fighters who raid Ardelian villages for captives and consider Lord-General Hasse theirs.

lore.title: Mercenary Companies
lore.text:
Eight mercenary companies are famous by name (the Gallowglass Company, the Black Kestrels, the Salt Lions, the Ninth Debt, the Ironmouth Free Company, the Hollow Hundred, the Gilt Banner, the Harvesters); hundreds more are not.
Pay is per soldier per day, plus provisions, death-pay and loot terms set in the contract. Standard terms: 90-day season contract; a quarter paid before marching, the rest monthly; death-pay of a month's wages to named kin; a third of the loot to the company; captives to the employer unless written otherwise. Bloodbound judges hear disputes when both sides accept them; otherwise the stronger side settles it.

lore.title: Gallowglass Company
lore.text: Bloodbound League heavy infantry: axes, polearms and mail, famous for holding a line past all reason. Motto: "We are paid to die slowly." Pay: 6-10 silver per soldier per day. Reputation: never break a contract, never take a second one against the same employer.

lore.title: Black Kestrels
lore.text: Crossbow skirmishers and scouts, mostly beastfolk and halflings, hired by every army that despises both. Motto: "Seen once." Pay: 4-8 silver per soldier per day. They take scouting, ambush and escort work and refuse siege duty.

lore.title: Salt Lions
lore.text: Sea mercenaries and marines of the Emerald Coast: boarding parties, convoy guards and harbor raiders. Motto: "The sea pays." Pay: 5-9 silver per day at sea. They work Vargate contracts more than they admit.

lore.title: The Ninth Debt
lore.text: A company of debt-slaves owned by Shackles' Grey Ledger, collared and fighting off their debts one contract at a time. Motto, said bitterly: "Paid in full." Hired cheaply, at 2-4 silver per soldier per day paid to the Ledger. Used as expendable vanguards and sent first into dungeons. Few ever work their debt off.

lore.title: Ironmouth Free Company
lore.text: Dwarven exiles from the Holds: siege engineers, sappers and heavy crossbowmen. Motto: "Every wall has a mouth." Pay: 1-2 gold per engineer per day. Ironanvil considers them oath-breakers; everyone besieging a fortress considers them indispensable.

lore.title: The Hollow Hundred
lore.text:
A company of Hollow-born who cannot awaken, fighting with numbers, crossbows, poison, nets and discipline. Motto: "Nothing to lose." Pay: 3-5 silver per soldier per day. Despised and underestimated; they have killed level 45 champions who did not take them seriously.
They absorb nothing from the dead they make, so no one can read their strength from their kills.

lore.title: The Gilt Banner
lore.text: Noble-born younger sons and daughters selling their lances: armored cavalry, expensive gear and manners. Motto: "Worth the price." Pay: 2-5 gold per lance per day. Favored by the River Confederacy, which prefers to rent its knights.

lore.title: The Harvesters
lore.text: A grim company that takes part of its pay in the enemy dead, which it sells to the Ashen Veil. Motto: "Nothing wasted." Pay: 3-6 silver per soldier per day plus corpse rights. Hired by employers who want deniable brutality; hunted by the Silver Mark.

lore.title: Bluewatch
lore.text:
Bluewatch: fortified River Confederacy watch village on the frontier road east of Auvoth, at the end of the Bluewatch Branch river route; the northernmost ordinary village in the known world. North of it lies nothing settled, only Wildzone and apex country.
Work: river inspection, convoy support, signal posts, ferries, storehouses, evacuation, frontier warning. People: tired, practical, armed, always listening for the signal horn.
Rule: a Watch-Captain answering to the River Council; not governed by Auvoth, Highmark or Shornmarch.
Places: the Watchhouse and its signal tower; a Guild branch desk in the Watchhouse, where newcomers register and read the job board; the inspection quay at the river-gate; storehouses; the Stray Oar (inn for convoy crews); the burial yard behind the Watchhouse, where the frontier's dead are burned or buried; no priest will live this far north, so Sister Temiwa heals and buries both.
Visitors notice: wet stone, smoke from the signal braziers, everyone looking north. Locals complain: late pay, Auvoth prices, Confederacy clerks who have never seen a stampede.
In August 611 low Wildzone beasts reached the Bluewatch road and the Border marches a season early.

lore.title: Auvoth
lore.text:
Auvoth: the Guild city around the sealed entrance to the Auvoth Depths; the northernmost city in the known world and the Adventurer Guild's capital.
In CY 384 Veyr the Unbound sealed the Depths and, the same winter, forced the surviving crowns to charter the Guild. The Auvoth Compact, sworn that year, put the city and the Depths in the Guild's keeping: no crown, Church office or army may own either.
Government: the Guild governs Auvoth and the Depths. The Guildmaster presides over the Compact Council, where every signatory realm keeps one representative: Highmark, River Confederacy, Holy Dominion (for the Church), Ironanvil, Ashmere, Valegard, Border Kingdoms; Startrace witnessed. The representatives advise, bargain and watch one another; the Guild decides. That seat is why every power keeps an embassy in a city none of them rules, and why the Guild counts as a transnational power in its own right. The Seventh Seal Court, in the tower over the seventh seal, rules on Depths permits, claims, seals and quarantines.
Law: the Guild's. Guild courts try crimes and disputes; Guild wardens keep the streets. The city extradites no one and honors no outside writ, warrant, bounty or debt claim.
Every great power wants Auvoth; none can take it without the others uniting against it and the Guild declaring a Withdrawal. Red line: foreign troops inside the walls. The Sealwardens hold the descents.
Visitors notice: lamps that never go out, Guild badges everywhere, how expensive everything is. Locals complain: adventurers who die owing money; crowns that want the city without its dead.
The Guild auctions its tithe and Sealwarden salvage at the Pale Market monthly; crowns bid through agents.
In August 611 the Depths gates surged at Auvoth; the Sealwardens held, and the Guild called it routine.

lore.title: Auvoth Depths
lore.text:
Auvoth Depths: the largest known leyline and the only mega-dungeon ever sealed by human hand. In CY 384, the Crownless Winter, Veyr the Unbound closed it with seven seals no one has been able to remake or fully read since; the seventh, the uppermost, lies under the Seventh Seal Terrace at the city's heart. Other great dungeons are walled, warded or abandoned; only the Depths were shut.
Below the seals is not a cave but a world. Each band has its own light, weather and seasons of circulation, its own plants, prey and predators, and food chains that never touch the surface: some creatures are born, breed and die there without ever rising, and some bands hold rivers, forests or open skies of glowing mana. Upper bands are the most worked and the most dangerous to complacency.
Veyr's seals divide the descent into bands, with controlled gates, collapsed transitions, ward barriers and quarantine layers between them. Entry requires a recorded party, a Guild permit matching the band's recommended clearance letter, and a recovery plan.
No band has ever been permanently cleared. What lies at the bottom, and what Veyr sealed in, is a sealed question; deeper bands are known only from broken records and survivors who will not talk about them.

lore.title: Highmark Capital
lore.text:
Highmark Capital: imperial throne city; walls within walls on a hill above the river, banners on every tower, heralds crying news in every square. The Iron Archive lies sealed beneath Crown Keep.
Rule: the Emperor through the Diet, War Office and city prefect. Sumptuary laws enforced; commoners kneel to passing nobles.
Visitors notice: bells, soldiers everywhere, prices that climb with every war. Locals complain: tax farmers, nobles' street duels, wages that never keep up.

lore.title: Thousand Sails
lore.text:
Thousand Sails: the River Confederacy's council seat and river-fleet hub, on islands and quays where the Grand Vein meets the Ledger River; masts thick as a forest.
Rule: the River Council, slowly and by vote. Everything is for sale; every sale is witnessed.
Visitors notice: noise, the smell of fish and tar, halfling cooks on every corner. Locals complain: tolls, councillors who never agree, fevers that start in Hulkrow.

lore.title: Ledgerford
lore.text:
Ledgerford: the Confederacy's northern banking city of stone counting-houses, guarded vaults and clerks in black.
It issues the bank notes the wealthy carry and holds more Highmark debt than anyone.
Visitors notice: the quiet, the guards, how carefully everyone speaks of money. Locals complain: crowns that borrow and never repay, Grey Ledger agents buying debts at the Steps, how hard it is to stay solvent in a city that counts everything.

lore.title: Holy City of Aurelion
lore.text:
Holy City of Aurelion: built around the First Brazier, the fire the Flamebearer lit, which has never gone out.
Rule: the High Pontiff and Conclave of Embers; the Dominion Chancellor runs everything practical.
Visitors notice: ash on the wind, bells for the dead every hour, pilgrims of every realm. Locals complain: pilgrims, rents, Inquest agents who ask too many questions; quieter voices, the Conclave's split.

lore.title: Ironanvil Citadel
lore.text:
Ironanvil Citadel: principal dwarven forge-city and traditional seat of the Council Beneath Stone, carved deep into the Dragonfang Mountains.
Visitors notice: heat, hammering that never stops, every dwarf able to recite their ancestors. Locals complain: grain prices, the Stone That Walks shifting their passes, the holds that went over to Ardelia.

lore.title: Battle Cry City
lore.text:
Battle Cry City: the United Chieftainates' council and Grand Muster city on the eastern plains.
Visitors notice: scars worn proudly, deed-names called across streets, herds driven through the center. Locals complain: Vargate's slavers on the coast, the Council's slowness to call a Muster.

lore.title: Abysswatch
lore.text:
Abysswatch: the Tidebound Covenant's council seat and naval command, a sea-fort city on a rock in open water.
Visitors notice: the sea always loud, every second family in mourning. Locals complain: the Black Trawl, Atlantis's reluctance with pilots, convoy taxes.

lore.title: Osterhal
lore.text:
Osterhal: Ardelia's capital in the central highlands; nine peoples' quarters around one great hall.
Rule: the Emperor and imperial chancery; the Knights of the Last Day guard the Hall and the count.
Visitors notice: dwarves, elves, orcs and spiritfolk sharing a street as equals; citizen tokens worn openly. Locals complain: election-season riots, Belisar's vote-sellers, Highmark's grip on the mouth of the Belis River.

lore.title: Ashkar
lore.text:
Ashkar: the Ashkaran capital, a city of mirrored glass that blazes at noon.
Visitors notice: the glare, veils on everyone, slaves outnumbering the free. Locals complain, quietly: the price of water, what the priest-surveyors read in the glass.

lore.title: Dragonfang Mountains
lore.text:
Dragonfang Mountains: vast high wilderness of storm cliffs, cloud seas, glaciers, dragon territories, dwarven gate-fortresses and ancient sanctuaries. The Stone That Walks roams the inner ranges; passes shift between surveys.
- Storm Cliffs: Dragonblood Pine, glacial rivers, Windcutter Pass, storm elementals, lightning spirits; Thunderpeak Summit, tied to the Hero's Trial and ruled by the dragon mortals call Kharuth, the Lightning Dragon King. Gateward Fortress guards the dwarven approaches.
- Cloudsea and Celestial Falls: permanent cloud seas, Celestial Cloudfall, floating sanctuaries, unstable ancient Light Bridges, white temple ruins, lost Star-Seeker knowledge.
- Silent Glaciers: the Dragonbone Wasteland, where residual dragon mana causes spatial and temporal anomalies; a glacier domain ruled by the dragon mortals call Morvhaal, the Ice Dragon King.
Resources: mithril, Storm-Infused Crystal, Thunderstone, Sky Crystal, Cloudlotus, dragonbone. Lethal off mapped routes.
Do: cross a pass, mine a vein, seek Thunderpeak. Want: Ironanvil wants the passes held; every crown wants dragonbone. Unknown: what the dragon kings want, and whether they speak.

lore.title: Witchwood Forest
lore.text:
Witchwood Forest: neutral magical forest about 100 km across in the Dragonfang's eastern foothills, under perpetual Bewitching Mist that distorts direction and defeats ordinary navigation. The Moonlight Compass is the only known reliable guide: under moonlight it points to the millennium-old tree beside the Witch's Cottage.
Grimface Trees bear twisted face-like bark; sentient treants guard the forest and obey the Witch, its sovereign, secluded there for centuries. She wants quiet, does not attack without cause, and punishes greed and disrespect.
Materials: Nightmare Bloom (dangerous hallucinatory plant); Ancient Treeheart Fragments (naturally shed wood heavy with life-attributed mana, prized for healing staves and protective talismans).
Do: find a Moonlight Compass, ask the Witch for something, pay what she asks. Want: healers want Treeheart; the Church wants to know what she is. Unknown: how old she is; whether she was ever human.

lore.title: Silent Giant Necropolis
lore.text:
In the Mythic Age the mountain-sized primordial Utum died in the western barrens. Over ten thousand years its body became a vast whale-fall ecosystem: flesh saturated with stable life-attributed mana rotted into fertile luminous soil; ribs form immense arches; the shattered skull shelters caverns and whole habitats.
Marrowvine draws mana from the bones; Stardust Lilies glow across the soil; Bonewalkers, slow and indifferent under bone-plated shells, graze the vines and crush whatever fails to move. Alchemists prize Behemoth Bone Powder. Life Crystals, pale-gold growths condensed near the ancient heart, are the finest healing material known. Legends say they restore the dead; they do not. They heal only the living.
Do: gather Life Crystals from the outer ribs, where they are small and rare, and sell them before someone takes them. Large crystals grow only near the heart, where mana is dense enough to sicken; few who go in come back. Want: Startrace wants to study the heart; Ashkaran caravans want crystals to sell to the Glass Regent; healers everywhere want them. Unknown: whether anything of Utum still lives in the heart.

lore.title: Wailing Battlefield
lore.text:
The Wailing Battlefield is where the First Abyssal Tide ended. Humans, elves and dwarves died here in such numbers that soil, weapons, armor and bones are saturated with death-frequency mana and repeated death patterns.
By day nearly silent: rusted weapons, shattered armor, war-beast skeletons, Rustgrass. By night, especially moonless, the patterns wake: corpses, bones and mana-forms reenact fragments of the battle and attack the living. They are echoes, never the spirits of the fallen. Rare formations grow complex enough to become intelligent high undead that shape curses, barriers and spells.
Grudge Crystals form here from repeated fear, rage and dying. Heroic Soul Steel: rare unrusted fragments carrying stable warding patterns left by disciplined defenders; no soul remains in the metal. The Grey Walker's range surrounds the field; where it passes, the battle goes still.
Do: scavenge Soul Steel and Grudge Crystals at the edges by day; survive the night if you misjudge. Want: the Ashen Veil wants Grudge Crystals; the Silver Mark wants the field contained; relic scavengers from Wailford want everything. Unknown: what the defenders were fighting at the very end. This is a sealed question.

lore.title: Hall of Heroes
lore.text:
Hall of Heroes: demiplane tied to the Hero's Trial and Thunderpeak in the Dragonfang heights. It holds no spirits (the dead end, heroes included), only mana patterned so densely by heroic deeds that the deeds persist as echoes.
Living challengers who pass the Hero's Trial may enter for a time and face those echoes: old battles, the weight of old choices, techniques of heroes long gone. Some return with clarified purpose or hard-won insight into a technique. Tales of a breakthrough in power are rumor: the Hall changes understanding, never level, and the Trial never bypasses training or a person's Vessel.
No mapped public approach: no road, gate or coordinate leads there; invent none. The approach is a locked discovery, reachable only through explicit campaign events, never casually.
Do: seek the Trial at Thunderpeak and survive whatever it is. Want: Startrace keeps watchers on the legend; every claimant to heroism wants to be seen to have entered. Unknown: how to reach it.

lore.title: Sea of the Ghost Fleet
lore.text:
In the Age of Kingdoms' Rise an unnatural mana storm annihilated the fleet of the Sons of the Sea God in battle with the early Confederacy. Storm, mass death, wrecks and command rituals left a self-sustaining field of death-frequency mana.
On moonless nights and in storms, spectral ships rise in their final formation. Lesser sailors repeat their duties without understanding; higher-complexity captains have accumulated stable identity, command lesser dead and work storm, fog and death mana like mages. Ships that provoke the fleet are destroyed; their dead join it. Instruments fail; direction, weather and magical sensing go wrong.
Passage custom: pour fine liquor into the sea, lower flags, pass in silence. Partly superstition, but the fleet's patterns sometimes read it as an old non-hostile signal and let compliant ships pass. The Black Trawl hunts the fleet's margins.
Materials: Fleet Banner Fragments (command patterns that can pacify or control undead); Fog of Lost Bearings (can be sealed and used to make disorienting fog).
Do: cross it, or salvage a banner fragment from a captain. Want: Tidebound wants a safe lane; the Ashen Veil wants a captain. Unknown: what made the storm.
Troubles: storms push lost ships into the fleet's field, and the Black Trawl takes what strays.

lore.title: Nameless Isle
lore.text:
Nameless Isle: at the heart of the Sea of the Ghost Fleet, wrapped in permanent magical fog (milky white by day, faintly silver at night) that distorts direction and the sense of time; those inside lose track of both.
A long-dead volcano dominates it, its collapsed summit a forest-filled caldera; sheer cliffs leave few landings. Grand ruins stand everywhere, said to be the final homeland of a lost civilization. Mana-bound stone-and-bronze custodians, sustained by old ritual seals, maintain them as if their kingdom never fell. Not hostile; they hold simple conversations but will not explain what they serve.
Materials: relics of the lost civilization (art, weapons, ritual diagrams, artisan plans); Condensed Time Dust, formed from the fog, prized for temporal research.
Do: find a landing, bargain with custodians, recover relics, leave before the fog takes the day or the boat. Want: Startrace and Atlantis both want the diagrams. Unknown: what lies at the caldera's heart, a locked discovery reachable only through explicit campaign events.

lore.title: Abyssal Throat
lore.text:
Abyssal Throat: black-rock atoll around a colossal pit covered by rune-inscribed slabs, the god-shackles the Exalted forged to bind Nyara.
Nyara: abyssal primordial whose true body is a mass of tendrils and parasitic propagation instincts; her spawn are the bloodline source of many tentacled monsters. Treat as eldritch body-horror and monster ecology, not erotica.
Her avatar: an adult silver-haired, crimson-eyed humanoid projection with its own will, curiosity about the surface and a taste for perilous games with those who reach the atoll. Bored, not a prisoner recruiting allies. Challengers who entertain it (by surviving its games, wit or spectacle) are paid in kind, and the games cost blood first: a Fragment of Nyara's Heart, an answer about the deep (never what lies on her prison floor), safe passage over the slabs, or a favor owed. The dull are discarded. The avatar never leaves the atoll or travels with anyone. Destroying rune slabs loosens the prison and courts a Tide.
Materials: Fragments of Nyara's Heart (chaotic power crystals shed during the sealing); Shards of the Star Shackles (remnants of the Exalted's restraints, formidable sealing power).
Do: entertain the avatar and survive its games. Want: Atlantis guards the slabs; the Ashen Veil would free her; Startrace wants a shard. Unknown: what lies on her prison floor. The Deep Bell roams the trench nearby.

lore.title: Winged Beasts Firmament
lore.text:
Winged Beasts Firmament: sky leyline of more than a dozen floating rock islands high above the forest on Verdantleaf's north-eastern edge, where it meets Thornheart, joined by ancient vines and natural stone bridges. Waterfalls pour from their edges into a permanent sea of mist. Each island holds a Heart of Wind Crystal shaping mana into a weight-lightening, wind-supporting field: natural magic, not reproducible.
A roost its flying creatures defend, some found nowhere else. Druids and beast tamers climb in to bargain or steal; most who take a mount lose a hand, a friend or the mount on the way down.
Materials: Heart of Wind Crystal Shards (light equipment, alchemy); Rainbow Serpent Feathers (fletching, luxury garments); Sky-Hanging Orchids.
Do: climb or fly in, take a mount, take shards. Want: every army wants flying mounts; druids want it left alone. Unknown: what would happen if a Heart were removed.

lore.title: Island of Lost Time
lore.text:
Island of Lost Time: restricted, fog-bound ruin island and possible Primordial Site north of the Deep Bell's trench. Old structures, broken clocks, warped stone halls and plants blooming on wrong cycles suggest ancient ritual interference with time.
No one in Arsveil can manipulate or reverse time; the island's effects are unstable ritual phenomena from ancient structures and dense mana. Dangers: lost navigation, time-disorientation, rumors of sudden aging or forgetting, ruin guardians, maps wrong by the time you read them.
Materials: Hourglass Sand (timing rituals, preservation charms); Momentbloom Pollen (from irregularly blooming flowers).
Do: land, gather, leave before you lose the day or the year. Want: Startrace wants measurements; the Deep Bell seems to want something nearby. Unknown: whether the island is a primordial.

lore.title: Mirage Spring Oasis
lore.text:
Mirage Spring Oasis: demiplane in the western barrens that cannot be sought. Rare accounts say it appears as a mirage to utterly lost travelers on the brink of despair, but despair never guarantees it; it cannot be predicted, invoked, farmed or relied on. Those who follow it may cross an invisible boundary into a real oasis of perpetual spring: clear lake, tall date palms, luminous flowers. Leaving is as elusive; some wake outside it after sleep, as if from a dream.
Descendants of a forgotten tribe live there, self-sufficient and wary. They shelter accidental visitors at a price: a day's labor in the groves per day of shelter, a story they have not heard, and an oath never to guide anyone back. They refuse to explain the oasis; oath-breakers never find it twice.
Materials: Mirage Spring Dates (finest travel provision known); Lotus of Tranquil Mind (valued in medicine and ritual).
Do: survive long enough to be found by it. Want: Ashkaran caravans would kill for a reliable route; there is none. Unknown: what the oasis is.

lore.title: Nareth, the Silent City
lore.text:
Nareth lies in the wild frontier south of Ardelia. In the Age of Kingdoms it was a city of about ten thousand; every inhabitant died in one night, without wounds.
Dense death-frequency mana has soaked it since, yet not one corpse has ever risen; no one knows why. Sound does not carry: voices die a few steps away; its bells never ring when struck. Bodies lie where they fell, untouched by rot.
The Church calls Nareth proof of the Flame; the Ashen Veil, the greatest crime in history. Ardelia patrols its edge from Oren and turns everyone back.
Do: slip past the patrols to recover a bell, a record or a body. Want: the Church wants a bell as a relic; the Veil wants to learn what stopped the dead. Unknown: what happened that night. This is a sealed question.

lore.title: Root-Tyrant
lore.text:
Root-Tyrant: great apex of Thornheart, the deep forest between Ardelia and Verdantleaf; treat as EG10: divert or flee. Signs: roads swallowed in a single season, trees that move toward fire, camps wrapped in roots by morning. Elves say the Reopening's roads woke it.
Troubles: the roads it swallows do not come back; caravans through the Thornheart now go armed and in daylight.

lore.title: Stone That Walks
lore.text: Stone That Walks: great apex of the inner Dragonfang Mountains; treat as EG10: divert or flee. Signs: passes that shift between surveys, peaks standing in different places from year to year, dwarven roads ending in sheer rock. People believe a mountain is walking toward something.

lore.title: Glass Crown
lore.text: Glass Crown: great apex of the glass wastes west of the Silent Giant Necropolis; treat as EG10: divert or flee. Signs: sand fused into glass in perfect rings, light from nowhere at night, caravans that vanish leaving their tracks. The Ashkaran Dominion believes it chose them and feeds it slaves.

lore.title: Long Thunder
lore.text: Long Thunder: great apex of the White-Horn March beyond the Frostbound Taiga (about y 215 to 260), never seen south of the taiga; treat as EG10: divert or flee. Sign: storms that travel against the wind, lightning that walks. It drives the mammoth herds south toward the Auvoth approaches; the White-Horn Clans follow its storms.

lore.title: Mother of Reeds
lore.text: Mother of Reeds: great apex of Sorrowfen, the great marsh east of Ardelia; treat as EG10: divert or flee. Signs: drowned villages left undisturbed, reed-dolls on doorsteps, songs across the water at dusk. Marsh villagers say she takes children and returns something else, and never say her name after dark.

lore.title: Deep Bell
lore.text: Deep Bell: great apex of the trench between the Abyssal Throat and the Island of Lost Time; treat as EG10: divert or flee.
